lessons.title: Shared responsibility model
lessons.short: In the cloud, security duties are split between the provider and the customer. The split depends on the service model (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS), but the customer always keeps responsibility for its data, identities, endpoints and configuration choices.
lessons.deep:
On-premises, your organization secures everything: the building, hardware, network, operating system, applications and data. Moving to the cloud hands some of that stack to the provider, which is the **shared responsibility model**.

- **IaaS** (Infrastructure as a Service, e.g. Azure VMs): the provider secures the physical datacenter, physical network and hosts. You manage the **operating system**, patching, apps, network controls you configure and data.
- **PaaS** (Platform as a Service, e.g. Azure App Service): the provider also runs the OS and runtime. You manage your application code, its configuration, access and data.
- **SaaS** (Software as a Service, e.g. Microsoft 365): the provider runs the whole application stack. You manage who has access, tenant settings and your data.

Whatever the model, the customer **always retains**: information and data, accounts and identities (including MFA and least privilege), devices/endpoints that connect, and the configuration choices made in the tenant. A misconfigured storage account or a phished admin account is still the customer's problem on a perfectly secured platform.

The rule of thumb: the further you move from on-premises toward SaaS, the more the provider handles, but accountability for data and identities never transfers.

terms.d: Framework that defines which security tasks the cloud provider handles and which the customer handles.
Infrastructure as a Service: provider runs physical hardware and hosts; customer runs the OS and everything above.
Platform as a Service: provider also runs the OS and runtime; customer manages app code, access and data.
Software as a Service: provider runs the full application; customer manages access, settings and data.

lessons.trap: Exams ask who patches the OS of an Azure VM: it is the customer (IaaS), not Microsoft; and data/identities are never the provider's responsibility in any model.
lessons.example: A company moves its file server to an Azure VM. Microsoft secures the datacenter, but the company must still patch Windows Server, configure the firewall rules and control who can read the files.

lessons.title: Shared responsibility for AI
lessons.short: AI workloads extend the shared responsibility model into three layers: AI platform, AI application and AI usage. The provider usually secures the platform and model hosting; the customer controls data access, identities, safe configuration, prompt injection mitigation and user policies.
lessons.deep:
AI systems add new risk because their behaviour can be steered by user prompts and by external data they read, and their outputs can drive real decisions. Microsoft describes three layers for an AI-enabled app:

- **AI platform**: infrastructure, the model, and platform safety controls such as **content filtering**.
- **AI application**: the app you build or deploy, its configuration, data sources, connectors and plugins.
- **AI usage**: how people use it, their inputs, acceptable use policies and oversight.

For SaaS AI (e.g. Microsoft 365 Copilot) or PaaS AI (e.g. Microsoft Foundry), the **provider typically handles** physical infrastructure, model hosting and platform-level safety controls.

The **customer typically handles**:
- What sensitive data the AI can reach (data protection and governance)
- Who can use the AI app and what they can do (identity and access)
- Safe configuration: connectors, data sources, logging, retention
- **Prompt injection** mitigation: an attacker hides instructions in input or in external content; counter with input validation, access controls and monitoring
- User training and acceptable use policies

As with classic cloud, using a higher-level AI service shifts work to the provider, but not accountability for your data or how the technology is used.

terms.d: Infrastructure, model and platform safety controls such as content filtering.
The app built on the model, its configuration, connectors, data sources and plugins.
How people use the AI: prompts, acceptable use policies and oversight.
Attack that embeds malicious instructions in user input or external data to manipulate an AI system.

lessons.trap: A tempting wrong answer is that the provider's content filtering fully covers prompt injection; securing connectors, data access and inputs remains the customer's job.
lessons.example: A firm builds a support bot in Microsoft Foundry that reads web pages. Microsoft hosts the model and filters harmful content, but the firm must restrict which sources the bot reads and monitor for injected instructions.

lessons.title: Defense-in-depth layers
lessons.short: Defense-in-depth uses multiple layers of security controls so that if one layer fails, the next still protects data. Microsoft lists seven layers from outermost to innermost: physical, identity and access, perimeter, network, compute, application, data.
lessons.deep:
**Defense-in-depth** is a layered strategy: instead of one big wall, many overlapping controls each slow an attacker and give defenders another chance to detect and respond. A single misconfiguration or vulnerability should not lead straight to a breach.

The seven layers, outermost to innermost:
- **Physical security**: locked datacenters, guards, badge readers, cameras.
- **Identity and access**: MFA, role-based access control (RBAC), Conditional Access checking location, device and risk.
- **Perimeter**: DDoS protection and perimeter firewalls at the network edge.
- **Network**: segmentation into zones, network security groups (NSGs) limiting traffic between resources.
- **Compute**: securing VMs and containers: patching, closing unused ports, restricting admin access.
- **Application**: secure development, input validation against SQL injection and XSS, security testing.
- **Data**: the innermost, most critical layer: access controls on data, encryption, classification.

The point for the exam is the idea of layering, and recognising which layer a given control belongs to.

terms.d: Security strategy using multiple overlapping layers of protection so no single failure exposes data.
Protects the network edge from large-scale attacks, e.g. DDoS protection and firewalls.
Azure rule set that allows or denies traffic between resources; a network-layer control.
Protection of VMs and containers through patching, port closure and restricted admin access.

lessons.trap: Exams mix up perimeter (DDoS, edge firewall) and network (segmentation, NSGs) layers; also remember data is the innermost layer, physical the outermost.
lessons.example: An attacker phishes a password (identity layer), but network segmentation stops lateral movement and the database is encrypted, so the stolen data is unreadable.

lessons.title: The CIA triad
lessons.short: Security goals are summarised by the CIA triad: confidentiality (only authorised people see data), integrity (data stays accurate and unaltered), and availability (data and systems are reachable when needed). Every control supports at least one of the three.
lessons.deep:
The **CIA triad** describes what defense-in-depth is protecting.

- **Confidentiality**: sensitive data (customer records, financial data, passwords, intellectual property) is visible only to authorised people. Controls: encryption, access controls, secure transmission. A breach of confidentiality means someone unauthorised read the data.
- **Integrity**: data stays accurate and complete and changes only through authorised processes. Threats include tampering, corruption by bugs, and unauthorised deletion. Controls: **cryptographic hashing**, **digital signatures**, audit logs, database transaction controls.
- **Availability**: authorised users can reach data and systems when needed. Threats: **DDoS attacks**, ransomware, hardware failure, natural disasters. Controls: redundancy, load balancing, failover, tested backups, DDoS protection.

The goals can conflict. Strong encryption boosts confidentiality, but if the key is lost the data becomes unavailable. Security teams balance the three according to how sensitive the data is and the business impact of each kind of failure.

terms.d: Only authorised parties can access the information.
Data remains accurate and unmodified except by authorised processes.
Data and systems are accessible to authorised users when needed.

lessons.trap: Hashing and digital signatures map to integrity, not confidentiality; DDoS and ransomware lockouts map to availability.
lessons.example: A hospital's records system is hit by a DDoS attack: no data is read or changed, but doctors cannot reach records, which is a failure of availability.

lessons.title: Zero Trust guiding principles
lessons.short: Zero Trust means "never trust, always verify": every request is authenticated and authorised no matter where it comes from. Its three guiding principles are verify explicitly, use least privileged access, and assume breach.
lessons.deep:
Traditional security trusted anything inside the corporate network. **Zero Trust** removes that assumption: every access request is checked as if it came from an open network.

**1. Verify explicitly**: always authenticate and authorise using all available signals, not just a password or network location. Signals include user identity, location, device and its compliance state, the app or service being accessed, data classification, and anomalies such as unusual sign-in times.

**2. Use least privileged access**: give the minimum access needed for the minimum time, via:
- **Just-in-time (JIT)** access: granted when needed, removed after.
- **Just-enough-access (JEA)**: only the specific permissions the task needs.
- **Risk-based adaptive policies**: automatically restrict access when risk is detected.

**3. Assume breach**: design as if an attacker is already inside. Segment access so one compromised account or device cannot reach everything (minimising the "blast radius"), encrypt end to end, and use monitoring and analytics to detect and respond quickly.

In Microsoft's products, Conditional Access is a key tool for verify explicitly, and Privileged Identity Management (PIM) supports JIT access.

terms.d: Security model that trusts no request by default and verifies every one, wherever it originates.
Authenticate and authorise using all available signals such as identity, location, device health and risk.
Least privilege techniques: access only when needed (JIT) and only the permissions needed (JEA).
Design as if attackers are inside: segment, encrypt end to end, and monitor to limit blast radius.

lessons.trap: Don't pick "trust devices on the corporate network": Zero Trust explicitly rejects location-based trust; and JIT/JEA belongs to least privilege, not verify explicitly.
lessons.example: An admin activates the Global Administrator role for two hours to fix an issue, then it expires automatically: least privileged access through just-in-time elevation.

lessons.title: Zero Trust foundational pillars
lessons.short: Zero Trust is applied across foundational pillars: identities, devices, applications, data, infrastructure and networks, tied together by visibility, automation and orchestration, which uses SIEM and SOAR to correlate signals and automate response.
lessons.deep:
Microsoft describes **six foundational pillars** of Zero Trust, plus an integrating layer. The six are sources of signals, places to enforce control, and resources to defend:

- **Identities**: users, services and devices. Identity is the primary control plane because most attacks abuse an identity; require strong authentication and least privilege.
- **Devices**: every device is an entry point; device health and compliance feed access decisions.
- **Applications**: how data is consumed; includes discovering unsanctioned **shadow IT** and controlling app permissions and consent.
- **Data**: classify, label and encrypt by sensitivity so protection travels with the data.
- **Infrastructure**: on-premises or cloud; assess configuration and versions, use JIT access to admin interfaces, use telemetry.
- **Networks**: segment, including **micro-segmentation** inside zones, encrypt end to end, real-time threat protection.

The integrating layer, **visibility, automation, and orchestration** (often counted as a seventh pillar), aggregates and correlates signals from the other six:
- **SIEM** (Security Information and Event Management) ingests and correlates data to detect threats, e.g. Microsoft Sentinel.
- **SOAR** (Security Orchestration, Automated Response) runs automated playbooks based on detections.

terms.d: Applications used without the IT department's knowledge or approval; discovered under the Applications pillar.
Dividing networks into small zones so a single compromise cannot move freely.
Security Information and Event Management: collects and correlates security data to detect threats.
Security Orchestration, Automated Response: automates response actions using playbooks.

lessons.trap: SIEM/SOAR correlation is the visibility, automation and orchestration pillar, not Infrastructure or Networks.
lessons.example: A company's SIEM correlates a risky sign-in (identity) with malware on the same laptop (device) and a SOAR playbook automatically disables the account.

lessons.title: Encryption: symmetric, asymmetric and data states
lessons.short: Encryption makes data unreadable without a key. Symmetric encryption uses one shared key; asymmetric uses a public/private key pair. Data is protected at rest, in transit (e.g. TLS) and in use (confidential computing).
lessons.deep:
**Encryption** converts readable data into ciphertext that is useless without the right **key**.

- **Symmetric encryption**: one key both encrypts and decrypts. Fast, so good for bulk data (disks, databases). Weakness: securely sharing that single key (**key distribution**).
- **Asymmetric encryption**: a mathematically linked **public key** and **private key**. Data encrypted with someone's public key can only be decrypted with their private key. Data signed with a private key can be verified with the public key. The public key can be shared freely, solving key distribution. Used in HTTPS and email encryption.
- **Digital signatures** (built on asymmetric keys) prove **authenticity** (who sent it) and **integrity** (unchanged since signing).

Data states:
- **At rest**: stored on disk, in a database or storage account.
- **In transit**: moving over a network; **TLS** protects HTTPS traffic; VPNs protect traffic over public networks.
- **In use**: being processed in memory/CPU. **Confidential computing** uses **secure enclaves** so data stays protected even from the OS or hypervisor.

**Key management**: store keys separately from data, use **hardware security modules (HSMs)**, rotate keys, restrict access. **Azure Key Vault** centrally stores keys, secrets and certificates.

terms.d: One shared secret key encrypts and decrypts; fast but hard to distribute safely.
Public key encrypts or verifies; matching private key decrypts or signs.
Data moving across networks, typically protected with TLS or a VPN.
Protects data in use by processing it inside hardware-based secure enclaves.
Cloud service for storing and managing keys, secrets and certificates.

lessons.trap: To send someone a confidential message you encrypt with THEIR public key; encrypting with your own private key is signing, which anyone with your public key can read.
lessons.example: A browser connects to a bank over HTTPS: TLS uses asymmetric keys to agree a session key, then fast symmetric encryption protects the data in transit.

lessons.title: Hashing and salting
lessons.short: Hashing turns any input into a fixed-length digest using an algorithm, with no key, and cannot be reversed. It is used to verify integrity and to store passwords; adding a unique random salt per password defeats rainbow-table attacks.
lessons.deep:
**Hashing** runs data through an algorithm to produce a **fixed-length** value called a **hash** or **digest**.

Key properties:
- **One-way**: you cannot recover the input from the hash. (Encryption, by contrast, is designed to be reversed with a key.)
- **No keys** are involved.
- **Deterministic**: the same input and algorithm always give the same hash, so a hash acts as a fingerprint. Change one character and the hash changes completely, which is why hashing supports **integrity** checks.

**Password storage**: systems store a password's hash, not the password. At sign-in, the typed password is hashed and compared to the stored hash. If the database leaks, attackers get hashes, not plain-text passwords.

Weakness: because hashing is deterministic, attackers precompute hashes of common passwords (**rainbow tables**, **dictionary attacks**) and look them up.

**Salting** fixes this: a unique random value (the **salt**) is added to each password before hashing. Two users with the same password get different hashes, and precomputed tables become useless. Salting is standard practice for secure password storage.

terms.d: Fixed-length output of a hashing algorithm, effectively unique to the input.
Random value added to each password before hashing so identical passwords produce different hashes.
Precomputed list of hashes for common passwords used to reverse-lookup unsalted hashes.

lessons.trap: Hashing is not encryption: it uses no key and is not reversible, and its output length is fixed regardless of input size.
lessons.example: A software vendor publishes a file's hash; after downloading, you hash the file yourself and compare to confirm it was not altered.

lessons.title: Governance, risk and compliance (GRC)
lessons.short: GRC brings together governance (rules and accountability that direct the organization), risk management (identify, assess, respond to and monitor threats) and compliance (meeting laws, regulations and standards). Compliance sets a minimum; it is not the same as security.
lessons.deep:
**GRC** is an integrated way to manage regulation, risk and accountability using policies, processes and technology.

**Governance**: the rules, practices and processes used to direct and control the organization. In security that means data classification and retention policies, identity standards, approval processes for privileged access, and clear ownership of controls. Governance is the structure that risk and compliance work inside.

**Risk management**: identifying, assessing and responding to threats to the organization's objectives. The aim is informed decisions, not zero risk.
- External risks: cyberattacks, natural disasters, regulatory change, suppliers.
- Internal risks: accidental data exposure, insider threats, fraud, process gaps.
- Process: **Identify**, **Assess** (impact and likelihood, giving a risk score), **Respond** (accept, mitigate, transfer such as insurance, or avoid), **Monitor**.

**Compliance**: adhering to the laws, regulations, standards and policies that apply because of industry, geography and data types, for example **HIPAA** (US health data), **ISO/IEC 27001** (information security management systems) and **SOC 2** (service organization audits).

Important: **compliance is not security**. A compliant organization can still have serious vulnerabilities.

terms.d: Rules, practices and processes that direct and control an organization, including accountability for controls.
Identifying, assessing, responding to and monitoring threats to objectives.
Adhering to the laws, regulations, standards and policies that apply to the organization.
Shifting a risk's financial impact to another party, e.g. buying cyber insurance.

lessons.trap: Buying insurance is risk transfer, not mitigation; and an organization that passes an audit is compliant, not automatically secure.
lessons.example: A retailer scores phishing as high likelihood and high impact, mitigates it with MFA, transfers residual cost with cyber insurance, and reviews the score each quarter.

lessons.title: Data residency, data sovereignty and data privacy
lessons.short: Data residency is about the physical location where data is stored and how it can move across borders. Data sovereignty means data is subject to the laws of the country where it is collected, held or processed. Data privacy is the proper handling of personal data.
lessons.deep:
Three compliance terms that are easy to confuse:

- **Data residency**: regulations about the **physical or geographic location** where data may be stored, and how and when it can be transferred, processed or accessed internationally. In the cloud, organizations must check which regions the provider stores data in.
- **Data sovereignty**: the concept that data is **subject to the laws and regulations of the country or region** in which it is collected, held or processed. Data collected in one country, stored in a second and processed in a third may fall under several legal regimes at once.
- **Data privacy**: appropriate handling of **personal data**, meaning any information relating to an identified or identifiable person. That includes direct identifiers (name, email, phone) and indirect identifiers (location history, browsing data). Privacy laws generally require transparency about collection and use, consent where required, individual rights (access, correction, deletion) and protection from unauthorised access.

Shortcut: residency = **where** it sits; sovereignty = **whose laws** apply; privacy = **how personal data is treated**.

terms.d: Rules about the physical location where data can be stored and how it may move across borders.
Data is subject to the laws of the country or region where it is collected, held or processed.
Proper handling of personal data: transparency, consent, individual rights and protection.
Any information relating to an identified or identifiable individual.

lessons.trap: If the question is about which country's laws govern data, answer data sovereignty; if it is about where data must physically be stored, answer data residency.
lessons.example: A New Zealand company requires all customer records to be stored in an Australian or NZ Azure region: that is a data residency requirement.

lessons.title: Identity as the primary security perimeter
lessons.short: Cloud apps, remote work, personal devices and partner access have eroded the network perimeter, so identity is now the primary security perimeter. Human, device, workload and agent identities must all be authenticated and authorised, across four pillars: administration, authentication, authorization and auditing.
lessons.deep:
Traditionally, organizations protected a **network perimeter** with firewalls and VPNs and trusted everything inside. That stopped working because of:
- **Cloud and SaaS apps** running outside the corporate network
- **Remote and hybrid work** from home and public Wi-Fi
- **Personal devices (BYOD)** the organization does not fully control
- **Partner and customer access** without joining the network
- **IoT devices** with hard-to-manage credentials

An attacker with a stolen VPN or cloud credential bypasses the perimeter entirely. So the key question becomes "who or what is asking, and should it be trusted?" That makes **identity the primary security perimeter**.

An **identity** is the set of attributes defining a person, device or software component. Types:
- **Human**: employees, contractors, partners, customers
- **Device**: laptops, phones, IoT sensors
- **Workload**: apps, services, containers, scripts calling APIs with no user involved
- **Agent**: AI agents acting for users or processes

The **four pillars of identity infrastructure**:
- **Administration**: creating, updating and removing identities (provisioning, deprovisioning) and the policies around them
- **Authentication**: proving the identity is genuine
- **Authorization**: deciding what it can access
- **Auditing**: recording who did what, when and where

terms.d: Set of attributes that define a person, device, service or agent.
Identity for software such as an app, service or container that accesses resources without a user.
Creating identities and access when people join, and removing them when they leave.
Tracking and recording identity activity: who did what, when and from where.

lessons.trap: Auditing is the pillar about logs and investigation, not verifying credentials (authentication) or granting permissions (authorization).
lessons.example: A salesperson works from a hotel on a personal tablet and opens Microsoft 365 directly over the internet; the firewall never sees the request, so the sign-in check is the real control point.

lessons.title: Authentication
lessons.short: Authentication (AuthN) proves an identity is who or what it claims to be, answering "who are you?". Credentials come from three factor types: something you know, something you have, something you are. MFA requires two or more factors from different categories.
lessons.deep:
**Authentication**, often shortened to **AuthN**, is the process of proving identity. The system challenges you for **credentials** and verifies them before allowing access.

A username alone proves nothing, because others can know it. A password helps but can be stolen, guessed or phished.

The three **authentication factor** categories:
- **Something you know**: password, PIN, security question
- **Something you have**: mobile phone with an authenticator app, hardware security key, smart card
- **Something you are**: biometrics such as fingerprint or facial recognition

**Single-factor authentication** (e.g. password only) is common but weak: if that factor is phished, the attacker becomes the user.

**Multifactor authentication (MFA)** requires **two or more factors from different categories**, for example a password plus approving a push notification on a registered phone. A password plus a security question is still just two "something you know" items, so it is not true MFA.

Authentication succeeds or fails. It confirms only **who** you are; it says nothing about **what** you can do, which is authorization.

terms.d: Proving that an identity is who or what it claims to be.
Evidence presented to prove identity, such as a password, key or biometric.
Sign-in requiring two or more factors from different categories.

lessons.trap: Two factors from the same category (password + PIN, or password + security question) do not count as MFA.
lessons.example: An employee types a password, then touches a fingerprint reader on a security key: something you know plus something you have/are, so MFA.

lessons.title: Authorization
lessons.short: Authorization (AuthZ) decides what an authenticated identity is allowed to do, answering "what can you access?". It always follows authentication and is based on roles, permissions and attributes, following the principle of least privilege.
lessons.deep:
**Authorization**, often shortened to **AuthZ**, determines what an authenticated identity may do: which apps, files, data or features it can use, and with what level of access (read, write, delete).

Decisions are usually based on:
- **Roles**: employee, manager, administrator (the basis of role-based access control, RBAC)
- **Permissions**: read, write, delete
- **Attributes**: department, location, job function

**Order and dependency**: authentication always happens first. You cannot evaluate permissions until you know who is asking. Authentication alone leaves resources exposed; authorization without verified identity has nothing reliable to check.

**Principle of least privilege**: give each identity only the minimum access needed for its job. This limits damage from a compromised account, reduces accidental data loss and supports compliance.

Microsoft's hotel analogy: showing ID at the front desk is authentication; the keycard that opens your room and the gym, but not other guests' rooms, is authorization.

terms.d: Determining what an authenticated identity is permitted to access or do.
Granting only the minimum access required for a task or role.
Authorization model that assigns permissions to roles, then roles to identities.

lessons.trap: If a user signs in successfully but gets "access denied" on a resource, that is an authorization outcome, not an authentication failure.
lessons.example: A new analyst can sign in to the finance app but only view reports; editing budgets is restricted to the Finance Manager role.

lessons.title: Identity providers, tokens and protocols
lessons.short: Modern authentication moves sign-in out of each app into a central identity provider (IdP), such as Microsoft Entra ID. The IdP verifies credentials and issues security tokens containing claims, using standard protocols: OpenID Connect, OAuth 2.0 and SAML.
lessons.deep:
With **modern authentication**, apps no longer keep their own passwords. They delegate authentication, authorization and auditing to an **identity provider (IdP)**, a central service that creates, maintains and manages identity information.

Sign-in flow:
1. The user opens an app.
2. The app redirects the user to the IdP.
3. The IdP verifies credentials (and MFA).
4. The IdP issues a **security token**.
5. The app, which **trusts** the IdP, validates the token and grants access.

Tokens carry **claims**: facts about the identity such as a unique ID, name, email, roles or groups, and issue/expiry times. Tokens are **time-limited**.
- **ID token**: proves the user signed in (authentication); tells the app who the user is.
- **Access token**: lets an app call a specific resource or API on the user's behalf (authorization).

Protocols:
- **OpenID Connect (OIDC)**: authentication for modern web and mobile apps, built on OAuth 2.0.
- **OAuth 2.0**: authorization; issues access tokens.
- **SAML**: XML-based, common for enterprise and legacy apps and cross-organization federation.

Examples of IdPs: Microsoft Entra ID, Google, Amazon, LinkedIn, GitHub.

terms.d: Central service that stores identities and provides authentication, authorization and auditing to apps.
Pieces of identity information inside a token, such as name, ID, roles and expiry.
ID token proves who signed in; access token grants access to a specific resource or API.
Standard protocols: OIDC for authentication, OAuth 2.0 for authorization, SAML for enterprise and federation.

lessons.trap: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization protocol; OpenID Connect adds the authentication layer on top of it. Tokens never contain the user's password.
lessons.example: A staff member opens an HR SaaS app, is redirected to Microsoft Entra ID, completes MFA, and returns with a token the HR app accepts.

lessons.title: Single sign-on (SSO)
lessons.short: Single sign-on (SSO) lets a user sign in once to a central identity provider and then access every application that trusts it without re-entering credentials. It improves user experience, reduces passwords, and lets admins remove access everywhere by disabling one account.
lessons.deep:
Without a central IdP, each app has its own accounts. That causes **fragmented credentials** (password reuse, weak passwords), **inconsistent policies** (MFA in some apps, not others) and **administrative overhead** (forgotten accounts left active after staff leave).

A central IdP lets the organization apply MFA and other policies once, monitor all sign-ins in one place, and manage the full lifecycle from provisioning to deprovisioning.

It also enables **single sign-on (SSO)**: the user authenticates once and is automatically signed in to every application that trusts that IdP, because each app accepts the IdP's token.

Benefits:
- **Better experience**: no separate credentials per app
- **Stronger security**: fewer password prompts means fewer phishing chances and less password reuse
- **Central control**: disabling one account in the IdP removes access to all connected apps immediately, making offboarding reliable

Don't confuse terms: **SSO** is about one sign-in across many apps that trust **one IdP**. **Federation** is a trust between **two separate IdPs** (often in different organizations). Microsoft Entra ID supports SSO to thousands of SaaS apps.

terms.d: Signing in once to access multiple apps that trust the same identity provider.
Configuration that makes an app (or another IdP) accept tokens from an identity provider.
Removing an identity's access when it is no longer needed, for example when an employee leaves.

lessons.trap: SSO reduces the number of passwords, it doesn't add one per app; and SSO within one IdP is not the same as federation between IdPs.
lessons.example: An employee signs in to Windows in the morning and opens Outlook, Salesforce and ServiceNow during the day without another password prompt.

lessons.title: Directory services and Active Directory Domain Services
lessons.short: A directory service stores information about users, devices, groups and other objects and answers who they are and what they can access. Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is Microsoft's on-premises directory, run on domain controllers, using Kerberos and NTLM.
lessons.deep:
A **directory** is a structured store of information about network objects: users, devices, groups, policies, applications. A **directory service** is the software that stores this data and makes it available to people and apps. It answers "who is this user, what groups are they in, what can they access?"

**Active Directory (AD)** is Microsoft's set of directory services, first released with **Windows 2000 Server**. Its best-known component is **Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS)**, which:
- Stores information about every member of a domain (users, computers, groups)
- Verifies credentials at sign-in
- Defines access rights to network resources

A server running AD DS is a **domain controller (DC)**.

With AD DS, organizations can:
- Give each user a single identity for many on-premises systems
- Use **Group Policy** to configure Windows devices centrally
- Authenticate users to on-premises apps using **Kerberos** and **NTLM**
- Organise objects into **organizational units (OUs)**

For many years AD DS was the foundation of identity in most organizations, built for Windows PCs on a corporate network running on-premises apps.

terms.d: Software that stores directory data about objects and makes it available to users and apps.
Active Directory Domain Services: Microsoft's on-premises directory service for domain-based networks.
A server running AD DS that stores the directory and authenticates sign-ins.
Authentication protocols used by AD DS for on-premises sign-in.

lessons.trap: AD DS is on-premises and uses Kerberos/NTLM; it does not natively speak OAuth 2.0 or OpenID Connect.
lessons.example: When an employee logs on to a domain-joined Windows PC at the office, a domain controller checks the password with Kerberos and applies Group Policy settings.

lessons.title: Limits of AD DS and Microsoft Entra ID
lessons.short: AD DS wasn't built for cloud apps, mobile devices, modern protocols or remote users. Microsoft Entra ID is Microsoft's cloud identity and access management service, delivered as Identity as a Service (IDaaS), and can connect to AD DS for hybrid identity.
lessons.deep:
AD DS was designed for an on-premises world, so it has limits today:
- **Cloud and SaaS apps**: AD DS doesn't natively authenticate users to them; extra sync tools or federation are needed.
- **Mobile devices**: no native management of iOS, Android and other non-Windows devices.
- **Modern protocols**: no native support for **OAuth 2.0** or **OpenID Connect**.
- **Remote access**: users off the corporate network usually need a VPN to reach a domain controller.

**Microsoft Entra ID** (formerly Azure Active Directory) is Microsoft's **cloud-based identity and access management** service, the cloud-era evolution of directory services.
- Delivered as **Identity as a Service (IDaaS)**: Microsoft runs the infrastructure; you manage users, devices, apps and policies.
- Supports modern, standards-based authentication (OIDC, OAuth 2.0, SAML).
- Works across platforms and device types.
- Connects to cloud and SaaS apps over the internet without a VPN.

**Hybrid identity**: organizations that already run AD DS can synchronize identities to Entra ID so users have one set of credentials for both on-premises and cloud resources. (The sync tools, Microsoft Entra Connect Sync and Cloud Sync, are covered in domain 2.)

terms.d: Microsoft's cloud identity and access management service, formerly Azure Active Directory.
Cloud-delivered identity service where the provider runs the infrastructure.
Linking on-premises AD DS with Microsoft Entra ID so users have one identity for both.

lessons.trap: Don't call it Azure AD on the exam; and Entra ID is not simply AD DS hosted in the cloud: it uses different, internet-friendly protocols.
lessons.example: A company with AD DS adopts Microsoft 365; it synchronizes users to Microsoft Entra ID so staff use the same password in the office and in Teams from home.

lessons.title: Federation
lessons.short: Federation creates a trust relationship between separate identity providers so a user can access another organization's or domain's resources with their home credentials. Trust is one-way unless two-way trust is explicitly configured. Examples: B2B partners, social sign-in, and AD FS.
lessons.deep:
**Federation** enables access to services across **organizational or domain boundaries** by establishing **trust relationships** between separate identity providers. The user authenticates with their own IdP and doesn't need a new account in the other organization.

Think passport control: your home country issues the passport and other countries accept it.

How it works: Organization A configures its IdP to **trust** Organization B's IdP. When a B user accesses an A resource, A accepts the authentication B already performed.

**Trust direction matters**: trust is **not automatically bidirectional**. If A trusts B, B does not automatically trust A; a two-way trust must be explicitly configured.

Common scenarios:
- **Business-to-business (B2B) collaboration**: partner staff use their own company credentials to reach a shared workspace or app.
- **Social and consumer identity providers**: "Sign in with Google, Microsoft or GitHub" in a customer app.
- **On-premises enterprise identity**: **Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS)**, a Windows Server role, lets AD DS users authenticate on-premises and receive tokens that cloud services accept.

Federation works across vendors because IdPs use standard protocols such as SAML, OpenID Connect and WS-Federation. Microsoft Entra ID supports all these scenarios.

terms.d: Trust between separate identity providers so users can access resources across boundaries with home credentials.
Active Directory Federation Services: Windows Server role that extends AD DS authentication to external and cloud services.
Letting users from partner organizations access your resources using their own identities.

lessons.trap: Federation trust is one-way by default; and federation (two IdPs) differs from SSO (one IdP, many apps).
lessons.example: Contoso's engineers sign in to Fabrikam's project portal with their Contoso accounts because Fabrikam's identity provider trusts Contoso's.

lessons.title: Microsoft Entra ID
lessons.short: Microsoft Entra ID is Microsoft's cloud-based identity and access management (IAM) service. Each organization gets a tenant: a dedicated directory of users, groups, apps and devices used to sign in to Microsoft 365, Azure and thousands of SaaS apps. It comes in Free, P1 and P2 editions.
lessons.deep:
Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure Active Directory) is an **identity as a service (IDaaS)** platform. When an organization signs up for a Microsoft commercial cloud service such as Microsoft 365 or Azure, it gets a **tenant**: a dedicated, trusted instance of Entra ID that holds its users, groups, devices and application registrations.

What it does:
- **Authentication**: verifies who is signing in (passwords, MFA, passwordless).
- **Authorization**: issues tokens using modern web protocols (OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, SAML) that apps trust.
- **Single sign-on (SSO)** to Microsoft 365, Azure and thousands of SaaS and on-premises apps.

It is not AD DS in the cloud: there are no domain controllers, OUs or Group Policy, and it doesn't rely on Kerberos/LDAP for cloud apps.

**Editions**:
- **Free**: included with Microsoft commercial online subscriptions; users, groups, SSO, security defaults.
- **P1**: adds Conditional Access, dynamic groups, SSPR with on-premises writeback (included in Microsoft 365 E3 and Business Premium).
- **P2**: adds Microsoft Entra ID Protection and Privileged Identity Management (included in Microsoft 365 E5).

The wider **Microsoft Entra** family also includes ID Governance, External ID, Verified ID, Workload ID and Global Secure Access (Internet Access and Private Access).

terms.d: A dedicated, trusted instance of Microsoft Entra ID representing one organization.
Identity as a service: identity and access management delivered from the cloud.
Paid editions; P1 adds Conditional Access, P2 adds ID Protection and PIM.

lessons.trap: Older material says Azure Active Directory; the current name is Microsoft Entra ID, and it is not the same as on-premises AD DS (no OUs, GPOs or domain controllers).
lessons.example: A startup buys Microsoft 365 Business Standard; a new Entra ID tenant is created automatically and every employee signs in to Teams and Outlook with an Entra ID account.

lessons.title: Users, guests and external identities
lessons.short: Human identities in Microsoft Entra ID are user accounts. Members are internal users (cloud-only or synced from AD DS); guests are external users invited through B2B collaboration. Microsoft Entra External ID covers B2B collaboration, B2B direct connect and external tenants for customer-facing (CIAM) apps.
lessons.deep:
**Users** can be created directly in the cloud (cloud-only) or synchronized from on-premises AD DS. Users are organized into **groups**: security groups (for access) and Microsoft 365 groups (for collaboration). Membership is either assigned or **dynamic** (rule-based, requires P1).

**Microsoft Entra External ID** handles people outside your organization:
- **B2B collaboration**: you invite a partner; a **guest** user object is created in your directory, but the guest authenticates with their own home identity provider (their Entra organization, a Microsoft account, Google, or an email one-time passcode). You never manage their password.
- **B2B direct connect**: a mutual trust between two Entra organizations, mainly for **Teams shared channels**. Users are **not** added as guests to your directory.
- **External tenant**: a separate tenant for apps you publish to consumers or business customers (**CIAM**). It supports self-service sign-up with email, one-time passcodes or social accounts such as Google and Facebook, plus custom branding.

Cross-tenant access settings control inbound and outbound B2B trust. External ID is billed on **monthly active users (MAU)**. Azure AD B2C is the legacy CIAM product and is no longer sold to new customers.

terms.d: An internal user of the organization, created in the cloud or synced from AD DS.
An external user invited via B2B collaboration who signs in with their home identity.
Mutual trust between Entra organizations, used for Teams shared channels; no guest object is created.
A separate tenant for customer-facing apps (CIAM) with self-service sign-up.

lessons.trap: B2B collaboration creates a guest object in your directory; B2B direct connect does not, and 'Teams shared channels' is the usual hint for direct connect.
lessons.example: Contoso invites an auditor from Tailspin as a B2B guest to a SharePoint site; she signs in with her Tailspin work account and Contoso never stores her password.

lessons.title: Workload identities
lessons.short: Workload identities are non-human identities given to software (apps, services, scripts, containers) so it can authenticate and access resources. In Microsoft Entra they are applications, service principals and managed identities. AI agents get dedicated agent identities through Microsoft Entra Agent ID.
lessons.deep:
Software needs an identity too. Microsoft Entra has three kinds of **workload identity**:
- **Application (app registration)**: the global *application object*, a template that describes the app, the tokens it can get and the APIs it needs.
- **Service principal**: the local instance of an application in a specific tenant. It defines what the app can do there and which resources it can reach. One is created in every tenant where the app is used.
- **Managed identity**: a special service principal that Azure manages for you, so developers **don't store or rotate secrets**.
  - **System-assigned**: enabled on one Azure resource, shares its lifecycle (deleted with it), can't be shared.
  - **User-assigned**: a standalone Azure resource that can be attached to many resources and must be deleted explicitly.

**Workload identity federation** lets external workloads (for example GitHub Actions) get Entra tokens without secrets. **Workload ID Premium** adds Conditional Access and ID Protection for workload identities and app health recommendations.

**Microsoft Entra Agent ID** extends identity to AI agents with *agent identities*, each with a human sponsor accountable for it.

terms.d: The local representation of an application in a tenant, holding its permissions there.
An Azure-managed service principal that removes the need to handle credentials.
Lets external workloads exchange a trusted token for an Entra token without secrets.
An Entra identity built specifically to authenticate an AI agent.

lessons.trap: If the stem says an Azure resource must access another resource without storing credentials in code, the answer is a managed identity, not an app registration with a client secret.
lessons.example: An Azure Function uses its system-assigned managed identity to read blobs from a storage account; no connection string or secret lives in the code.

lessons.title: Device identities
lessons.short: A device identity is a device object in Microsoft Entra ID. Devices can be Microsoft Entra registered (personal/BYOD), Microsoft Entra joined (organization-owned, cloud-joined Windows) or Microsoft Entra hybrid joined (joined to AD DS and registered in Entra ID). Device identity enables device-based Conditional Access and Intune management.
lessons.deep:
Devices are a second kind of non-human identity. Entra ID offers three ways to give a device an identity:
- **Microsoft Entra registered**: for **bring-your-own-device (BYOD)** and mobile devices (Windows, iOS, Android, macOS). The user keeps signing in to the device with a personal/local account but adds a work account to reach apps.
- **Microsoft Entra joined**: for **organization-owned** Windows 10/11 devices (and Windows Server 2019+ VMs in Azure). Users sign in to the device with their Entra ID account and get SSO to cloud and on-premises resources. No on-premises domain needed.
- **Microsoft Entra hybrid joined**: devices joined to **on-premises AD DS** and also registered in Entra ID. A transition step for organizations that still rely on AD and Group Policy.

All three can coexist. Once a device has an identity, admins can manage it with **Microsoft Intune**, mark it **compliant**, and use Conditional Access grant controls such as *Require device to be marked as compliant* or *Require Microsoft Entra hybrid joined device*.

terms.d: Personal or mobile devices registered for access to work resources.
Organization-owned devices joined directly to Entra ID; users sign in with Entra accounts.
Devices joined to on-premises AD DS and registered in Entra ID.

lessons.trap: BYOD = registered; company-owned cloud-only = joined; existing domain-joined PCs = hybrid joined. Mixing up joined and hybrid joined is the common mistake.
lessons.example: A company keeps its existing domain-joined desktops as hybrid joined while new laptops shipped to remote staff are Microsoft Entra joined straight out of the box.

lessons.title: Hybrid identity: synchronization
lessons.short: Hybrid identity gives users one identity across on-premises AD DS and Microsoft Entra ID. Synchronization copies users, groups and other objects from AD DS to Entra ID using Microsoft Entra Connect Sync (an on-premises sync server) or Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync (lightweight agents with configuration held in the cloud).
lessons.deep:
Many organizations still run **Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS)** on-premises. **Hybrid identity** means users get a common identity for on-premises and cloud resources. It relies on **provisioning** (creating, updating and deleting objects) and **synchronization** (keeping on-premises and cloud copies matched).

Two Microsoft tools sync AD DS to Entra ID:
- **Microsoft Entra Connect Sync**: software installed on an on-premises Windows server. It also configures the sign-in method (PHS, PTA or federation with AD FS) and features like password writeback. **Microsoft Entra Connect Health** monitors it.
- **Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync**: a lightweight **provisioning agent** on-premises with outbound-only connections; configuration lives in the Entra admin center. Multiple active agents give high availability, and it can sync **multiple disconnected forests** into one tenant, useful after mergers.

For synced users, AD DS is normally the **source of authority**, so admins edit attributes on-premises and the change flows to the cloud. Hybrid identity features are included at no extra cost.

terms.d: On-premises server software that syncs AD DS objects to Entra ID.
Cloud-managed sync using lightweight on-premises provisioning agents.
The directory where an object is mastered and edited (usually AD DS for synced users).

lessons.trap: Don't confuse the sync tool (Connect Sync or Cloud Sync) with the sign-in method (PHS, PTA, federation); Microsoft Entra Domain Services is not a sync tool for hybrid identity.
lessons.example: After acquiring a company with its own disconnected AD forest, IT deploys Cloud Sync agents in both forests to bring all users into a single Entra tenant.

lessons.title: Hybrid identity: PHS, PTA and federation
lessons.short: Hybrid users authenticate in one of three ways: password hash synchronization (PHS) validates a hash of the password hash in the cloud; pass-through authentication (PTA) validates passwords against on-premises AD DS through agents; federation hands authentication to a trusted IdP such as AD FS. Microsoft recommends enabling PHS even as a backup.
lessons.deep:
**Password hash synchronization (PHS)**: Entra Connect syncs a hash of each user's password hash to Entra ID, which then validates sign-ins in the cloud. It needs the least infrastructure, keeps working if on-premises is down, and is required for ID Protection's **leaked credentials** detection.

**Pass-through authentication (PTA)**: Entra ID receives the sign-in, but the password is validated against on-premises AD DS by lightweight **authentication agents** that use outbound connections only (Microsoft recommends three for availability). Because AD DS checks each sign-in, on-premises policies like disabled accounts, password expiry and logon hours are enforced immediately. Passwords are never validated in the cloud.

**Federation**: Entra ID redirects authentication to a trusted federation system, typically **AD FS** (multiple AD FS servers plus Web Application Proxy servers in the perimeter network). Choose it for needs such as a third-party MFA that requires a federated IdP, or sign-in with sAMAccountName. It is the most complex to run.

**Seamless SSO** works with PHS and PTA to avoid extra prompts on domain-joined devices.

terms.d: Password hash synchronization: a hash of the password hash is synced and validated in the cloud.
Pass-through authentication: on-premises agents validate passwords against AD DS.
Entra ID trusts an external IdP, such as AD FS, to authenticate users.
Automatic sign-in for users on domain-joined devices on the corporate network.

lessons.trap: Leaked-credential detection needs PHS; if the stem demands on-premises policies enforced at every sign-in with no perimeter servers, the answer is PTA, not federation.
lessons.example: A bank must enforce AD logon hours for cloud sign-ins but refuses to run servers in its DMZ, so it chooses PTA and also enables PHS as a backup.

lessons.title: Authentication methods
lessons.short: Authentication proves who you are. Microsoft Entra ID supports passwords plus methods such as SMS, voice call, Microsoft Authenticator (push notifications, passwordless phone sign-in, passkeys), software and hardware OATH tokens and email one-time passcodes. Admins enable methods for users and groups in the Authentication methods policy.
lessons.deep:
**Passwords** are the most common and weakest method: they can be guessed, sprayed, phished and reused across sites.

Other methods in Microsoft Entra ID:
- **SMS**: a code sent by text; usable for MFA and SSPR, and as a primary method when **SMS sign-in** is enabled.
- **Voice call**: an automated call; usable for MFA and SSPR only, **not** as a primary sign-in method.
- **Microsoft Authenticator**: push notifications with **number matching** (the user types the number shown on screen), passwordless phone sign-in, passkeys, and one-time codes.
- **OATH tokens**: **software** (an authenticator app showing a time-based one-time passcode, TOTP) or **hardware** (a key-fob that displays a code).
- **Email one-time passcode**: for SSPR by members and for guest sign-in.

Some methods are **primary** (first factor), some **secondary** (MFA only), some both. Methods are managed centrally in the **Authentication methods policy**, which has replaced method management in the legacy MFA and SSPR policies. Microsoft rates Authenticator and passkeys as stronger than SMS and voice, which are exposed to SIM-swap and interception.

terms.d: The first factor used to sign in, such as a password or passkey.
A time-based one-time passcode generated by an app or hardware token.
Authenticator push requires typing the number shown on the sign-in screen.
Central policy where admins enable methods for users and groups.

lessons.trap: Voice call can't be a primary sign-in method; SMS and voice are the weakest phone methods, so they're the wrong answer when the stem asks for the most secure option.
lessons.example: An admin enables Microsoft Authenticator for all users and limits SMS to a small group of frontline workers who don't have smartphones.

lessons.title: Passwordless methods and Temporary Access Pass
lessons.short: Passwordless methods replace the password with something you have plus a PIN or biometric. Microsoft Entra ID supports Windows Hello for Business, passkeys (FIDO2 security keys or passkeys in Microsoft Authenticator), Authenticator phone sign-in and certificate-based authentication. A Temporary Access Pass helps users onboard or recover them.
lessons.deep:
Passwordless sign-in is both more secure and easier.
- **Windows Hello for Business (WHfB)**: a credential bound to a specific Windows device; a **PIN or biometric** (face, fingerprint) unlocks a private key. The PIN stays on the device and is never sent to a server.
- **Passkeys (FIDO2)**: public/private key pairs stored on a hardware security key, in Microsoft Authenticator, or synced by a platform. The key is bound to the website's origin, so it can't be replayed on a phishing site.
- **Microsoft Authenticator phone sign-in**: approve the sign-in on the phone with a number match and biometric/PIN.
- **Certificate-based authentication (CBA)**: X.509 certificates, such as smart cards, validated directly by Entra ID without AD FS.

**Phishing-resistant** methods are passkeys (FIDO2), WHfB and multifactor CBA.

**Temporary Access Pass (TAP)**: a time-limited passcode (configurable from 10 minutes to 30 days, single- or multi-use) that an Authentication Administrator issues so a user can sign in and register a passwordless method on day one or after losing a device.

terms.d: Device-bound credential unlocked by PIN or biometrics on Windows.
Phishing-resistant key-pair credential on a security key or authenticator.
Sign-in with an X.509 certificate, such as a smart card.
Time-limited passcode used to onboard or recover passwordless methods.

lessons.trap: Phishing-resistant means passkeys/FIDO2, Windows Hello for Business or certificate-based authentication; Authenticator push and SMS are not phishing-resistant.
lessons.example: A new hire receives a Temporary Access Pass from the helpdesk, signs in once and registers a passkey in Microsoft Authenticator, never needing a password.

lessons.title: Multifactor authentication (MFA)
lessons.short: Multifactor authentication (MFA) requires two or more different factor types: something you know (password, PIN), something you have (phone, security key) and something you are (fingerprint, face). Microsoft Entra enforces MFA through security defaults, Conditional Access and ID Protection risk policies; authentication strengths define which methods count.
lessons.deep:
A **factor** is a category of evidence:
- **Something you know**: password, PIN.
- **Something you have**: phone with Authenticator, OATH token, security key.
- **Something you are**: biometrics such as fingerprint or face.

MFA needs at least **two different categories**. A password plus a security question is two things you know, so it is **not** MFA.

**Microsoft Entra MFA** can use Authenticator push (with number matching to resist *MFA fatigue* push-bombing), OATH codes, SMS, voice, or passkeys. Users register methods once through combined security info registration.

Ways to require MFA:
- **Security defaults** (free, all-or-nothing).
- **Conditional Access** policies (P1), the recommended, granular approach.
- **ID Protection** sign-in risk policies (P2).

**Authentication strengths** in Conditional Access specify which method combinations satisfy a policy. Built-in strengths are **MFA strength**, **Passwordless MFA strength** and **Phishing-resistant MFA strength**; admins can also create custom strengths. Microsoft also enforces MFA for sign-in to admin portals such as the Azure portal.

terms.d: A category of proof: something you know, have or are.
Attack that floods users with push prompts hoping one is approved.
Conditional Access control defining which method combinations are allowed.

lessons.trap: Two items from the same category (password + PIN, password + security question) are not MFA; the exam often hides this in an option.
lessons.example: Contoso requires the Phishing-resistant MFA strength for all admin role holders, so admins must use passkeys or Windows Hello for Business.

lessons.title: Security defaults
lessons.short: Security defaults are a free, single-switch set of identity protections in Microsoft Entra ID: all users register for MFA, administrators do MFA at every sign-in, users do MFA when needed, legacy authentication is blocked and privileged activities like the Azure portal require MFA. They're enabled by default in new tenants.
lessons.deep:
Not every organization has P1 licences or time to design policies. **Security defaults** give a baseline at no cost.

What they enforce:
- **All users register for MFA** (Microsoft Authenticator by default).
- **Administrators** in key roles (Global, Security, Conditional Access, Exchange, SharePoint, User Administrator and others) must perform MFA **every sign-in**.
- **Users** are prompted for MFA when Entra ID judges it necessary.
- **Legacy authentication** (older protocols such as POP, IMAP and SMTP basic auth that can't do MFA) is **blocked**.
- **Privileged activities** such as the Azure portal, Azure PowerShell and Azure CLI require MFA.

Tenants created on or after 22 October 2019 have them on automatically.

Limits: they are all-or-nothing, with no custom exclusions, locations or app targeting. **Security defaults and Conditional Access can't be used together**: an organization with P1 that wants granular policies must turn security defaults off and recreate the protections in Conditional Access (Microsoft-managed policies help).

terms.d: Free preconfigured identity protections enabled with one switch.
Older protocols using basic auth that can't perform MFA.
Conditional Access policies Microsoft creates to replicate baseline protections.

lessons.trap: When a stem needs exceptions, named locations or targeting specific apps, the answer is Conditional Access, and security defaults must be disabled first.
lessons.example: A 20-person charity with only free Entra ID licences leaves security defaults on, giving everyone MFA and blocking legacy email protocols without writing any policy.

lessons.title: Self-service password reset (SSPR)
lessons.short: Self-service password reset (SSPR) lets users reset a forgotten password or unlock their account without calling the helpdesk, after verifying with one or two registered methods. For hybrid users, password writeback sends the new password back to on-premises AD DS.
lessons.deep:
**Password change** means you know your current password and choose a new one. **Password reset** means you forgot it and must prove your identity another way. **SSPR** handles reset and account unlock.

How it works:
- Admins enable SSPR for selected users or all users and require **one or two methods** to reset.
- Users register methods (Authenticator, SMS, voice call, OATH code, email, security questions) through combined registration, and can be prompted to reconfirm them periodically.
- At sign-in the user selects *Forgot my password*, verifies with the required methods and sets a new password that must pass password protection checks.
- Users and admins can be notified when a reset happens.
- Admin accounts get a stricter **two-gate** policy (two methods, no security questions).

**Password writeback** (configured with Microsoft Entra Connect or Cloud Sync) writes cloud resets back to AD DS, so hybrid users can reset once and use the password everywhere.

**Licensing**: cloud-only password change works with Entra ID Free; SSPR reset needs Entra ID P1/P2 or Microsoft 365 Business Standard/Premium; writeback needs P1/P2 or Business Premium.

terms.d: Self-service password reset: users reset or unlock their own accounts.
Writes cloud password changes and resets back to on-premises AD DS.
Stronger SSPR rule for admins requiring two verification methods.

lessons.trap: Hybrid users can't use SSPR for their on-premises password unless password writeback is enabled; and reset (not change) needs at least P1.
lessons.example: On a Saturday a synced user forgets her password, resets it through SSPR with an Authenticator approval and an SMS code, and writeback lets her unlock her domain laptop on Monday.

lessons.title: Password protection and smart lockout
lessons.short: Microsoft Entra Password Protection blocks weak passwords using a global banned password list maintained by Microsoft and an optional custom banned password list of up to 1,000 organization-specific terms. Smart lockout locks out attackers guessing passwords while letting the real user keep working. Both protections can extend to on-premises AD DS.
lessons.deep:
**Microsoft Entra Password Protection** checks new passwords when users change or reset them.
- **Global banned password list**: built by Microsoft from Entra security telemetry, applied automatically to all users; it **can't be edited or disabled**.
- **Custom banned password list**: up to **1,000** base terms specific to you (brand names, products, locations, local sports teams). Requires **P1 or P2**.

The algorithm normalizes passwords (lowercase; 0 becomes o, @ becomes a, $ becomes s), fuzzy-matches banned terms, checks the user's name and tenant name, then scores the result; a password needs **at least 5 points** to be accepted. So variations like *C0nt0s0!* are still blocked.

**On-premises**: install the **DC agent** on domain controllers plus the **proxy service** to enforce the same lists for AD DS password changes (start in audit mode, then enforce).

**Smart lockout** is always on. It tracks failed sign-ins and locks the account temporarily (by default after 10 failed attempts, for 60 seconds, increasing on repeat), and tries to tell familiar locations from attackers. Customizing threshold and duration needs P1.

terms.d: Microsoft-maintained list of weak passwords applied to everyone.
Up to 1,000 organization-specific terms you block (P1/P2).
Temporary lockout that targets attackers while sparing the genuine user.
Service on domain controllers that enforces Password Protection in AD DS.

lessons.trap: The custom list is not meant for huge breach dumps (1,000-term limit) and the global list can't be edited; protecting AD DS needs the on-premises DC agent, not password writeback.
lessons.example: Fabrikam adds 'fabrikam', 'widget' and 'seattle' to the custom banned list, so 'F@brikam2026!' is rejected in the cloud and on domain controllers.

lessons.title: Conditional Access: signals and decisions
lessons.short: Conditional Access is Microsoft Entra ID's policy engine: if-then policies that combine signals (user or group, location, device, application, real-time risk) to make an access decision (block, grant, or grant with requirements such as MFA). Policies are evaluated after first-factor authentication and are central to Zero Trust.
lessons.deep:
A Conditional Access policy reads like **if this, then that**: *if* a user in Finance signs in to the payroll app from outside the office, *then* require MFA.

**Assignments (the 'if')**:
- **Users, groups, directory roles, guests**, and with Workload ID Premium, **workload identities**.
- **Target resources**: cloud apps, user actions (such as registering security info) or authentication contexts.
- **Conditions**: **sign-in risk** and **user risk** from ID Protection (P2), **device platforms**, **locations** (named locations by IP range or country/region), **client apps** (for example legacy authentication) and **filter for devices**.

**Access controls (the 'then')**: **block access**, or **grant access** optionally requiring controls.

Key behaviour:
- Policies are enforced **after first-factor authentication**, so CA isn't a first-line defence against denial-of-service.
- All applicable policies apply together; every requirement must be met, and **Block wins** over grant.
- Exclude **emergency access accounts** so you can't lock yourself out.

terms.d: Information CA evaluates, such as user, location, device, app or risk.
A defined IP range or set of countries/regions used as a CA condition.
The 'who and what' a policy applies to: users, resources and conditions.

lessons.trap: Conditional Access runs after the first factor succeeds; when several policies apply, all requirements combine and a Block policy overrides any grant.
lessons.example: A policy blocks all sign-ins from countries where Contoso has no staff, while a second policy requires MFA for every sign-in to the HR app.

lessons.title: Conditional Access: grant and session controls
lessons.short: Conditional Access grant controls block access or grant it with requirements: MFA, an authentication strength, a compliant device, a Microsoft Entra hybrid joined device, an app protection policy, a password change or terms of use. Session controls limit the experience after sign-in. Conditional Access requires Microsoft Entra ID P1.
lessons.deep:
**Grant controls** decide whether access is allowed:
- Block access, or grant with: require MFA, require authentication strength, require compliant device, require Microsoft Entra hybrid joined device, require app protection policy, require password change, require terms of use. (The older *Require approved client app* grant was retired in 2026; use *Require app protection policy* instead.)
- With several controls you choose **require all** or **require one**.

**Session controls** shape what happens after sign-in:
- **Sign-in frequency**: how often users must reauthenticate.
- **Persistent browser session**: whether users stay signed in after closing the browser.
- **Application enforced restrictions**: apps such as SharePoint give limited access to unmanaged devices.
- **Conditional Access App Control**: routes sessions through **Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps** as a reverse proxy for real-time monitoring and control (for example block downloads).
- Continuous access evaluation (CAE) settings and **token protection**.

**Operations**: start policies in **report-only** mode to see impact without enforcing, and use the What If tool to test. Conditional Access needs **P1**; risk-based conditions need **P2**. If a licence lapses, policies remain but can't be edited.

terms.d: Requirement that must be met before access is allowed, such as MFA.
Restriction applied after sign-in, such as sign-in frequency.
Policy evaluates and logs results without enforcing them.
Session control proxying traffic via Defender for Cloud Apps.

lessons.trap: Sign-in frequency and App Control are session controls, not grant controls; CA itself needs P1, but sign-in/user risk conditions need P2.
lessons.example: Before enforcing 'require compliant device' for everyone, an admin runs it in report-only mode for two weeks and reviews which sign-ins would have failed.

lessons.title: Microsoft Entra built-in roles
lessons.short: Microsoft Entra built-in roles grant administrative permissions over Entra ID and Microsoft services, such as Global Administrator, User Administrator, Helpdesk Administrator and Global Reader. Follow least privilege: assign the narrowest role, keep fewer than five Global Administrators, and keep two cloud-only emergency access accounts.
lessons.deep:
Admin tasks are delegated with **Microsoft Entra roles**. Built-in roles fall into three groups:
- **Microsoft Entra-specific roles**: manage Entra resources only, e.g. **User Administrator**, **Groups Administrator**, **Application Administrator**, **Helpdesk Administrator** (reset passwords and invalidate refresh tokens for non-admins).
- **Service-specific roles**: manage one Microsoft 365 service, e.g. **Exchange Administrator**, **SharePoint Administrator**, **Intune Administrator**, **Teams Administrator**.
- **Cross-service roles**: span services, e.g. **Global Administrator** (almost everything), **Global Reader** (read-only version of Global Admin), **Security Administrator**, **Security Reader**, **Compliance Administrator**.

**Privileged Role Administrator** manages role assignments and PIM settings. Built-in roles' permissions **can't be changed**.

Microsoft best practice:
- **Least privilege**: choose the narrowest role and scope.
- **Fewer than five Global Administrators**.
- **Two cloud-only emergency access (break-glass) accounts** with Global Administrator, excluded from normal policies.
- Use **cloud-only accounts** for admin roles, not synced on-premises accounts.
- Use **PIM** for just-in-time access.

terms.d: Role with access to nearly all admin features across Entra and Microsoft services.
Read-only counterpart of Global Administrator.
Manages role assignments and Privileged Identity Management.
Cloud-only break-glass admin account for when normal admins are locked out.

lessons.trap: When a stem asks for read-only visibility, Global Reader or Security Reader is right; Global Administrator 'because it works' violates least privilege.
lessons.example: Service desk staff get Helpdesk Administrator so they can reset user passwords, while only three senior engineers hold Global Administrator through PIM.

lessons.title: Role-based access control model
lessons.short: Microsoft Entra RBAC grants permissions through role assignments: a role definition (set of permissions) assigned to a security principal (user, role-assignable group or service principal) at a scope (tenant, administrative unit or a specific resource). Custom roles need P1. Entra roles manage directory objects; Azure RBAC roles manage Azure resources.
lessons.deep:
**RBAC** means permissions come from roles, not from individual grants. A **role assignment** has three parts:
- **Security principal**: who gets access (user, role-assignable group, service principal).
- **Role definition**: what they can do, a collection of permissions. Either **built-in** (fixed) or **custom** (built from the same permission list; needs **P1** for users assigned them).
- **Scope**: where it applies: the whole **tenant**, an **administrative unit** (a container of users/groups/devices, e.g. one region or department), or a single **resource** such as one app registration.

Assign roles to **role-assignable groups** (P1) to manage access by membership, and use **PIM** (P2) for just-in-time activation.

**Entra RBAC vs Azure RBAC**: same model, different planes.
- **Entra roles** (Global Administrator, User Administrator...) control Entra resources such as users, groups and apps via Microsoft Graph.
- **Azure roles** (**Owner, Contributor, Reader, User Access Administrator**) control Azure resources at management group, subscription, resource group or resource scope via Azure Resource Manager.

Owning a subscription does not let you create Entra users, and vice versa.

terms.d: A named collection of permissions.
Attaching a role definition to a principal at a scope.
The set of resources the assignment applies to.
Container that limits an Entra role's scope to a subset of objects.

lessons.trap: Owner, Contributor and Reader are Azure RBAC roles for Azure resources; to limit Entra admins to a department, use administrative units, not management groups.
lessons.example: Contoso creates an administrative unit for its German users and gives the Berlin helpdesk the Helpdesk Administrator role scoped to that unit only.

lessons.title: Microsoft Entra ID Governance and the identity lifecycle
lessons.short: Microsoft Entra ID Governance makes sure the right people have the right access to the right resources at the right time, and that auditors can prove it. It covers the identity lifecycle (joiner, mover, leaver), access lifecycle and privileged access with lifecycle workflows, entitlement management, access reviews and PIM.
lessons.deep:
**Identity governance** answers four questions: which identities should have access to which resources; what they are doing with it; whether there are controls for managing access; and whether auditors can verify the controls work.

**Identity lifecycle** (joiner, mover, leaver):
- **Joiner**: inbound provisioning from HR systems (Workday, SAP SuccessFactors) creates accounts in AD DS or Entra ID so new staff are productive on day one.
- **Mover**: attribute changes (new department) update group and app access.
- **Leaver**: access is removed and the account disabled, then deleted.

**Lifecycle workflows** automate these events using templates and triggers such as the employee hire date or leave date: generate a **Temporary Access Pass** and email it to the manager before day one, send a welcome email, add to groups, remove from groups and disable the account on the last day. **App provisioning** (for example via SCIM) creates and removes accounts in SaaS apps.

**Licensing**: Entra ID Governance (or Microsoft Entra Suite) on top of P1/P2. PIM and core access reviews/entitlement management also work with P2, but **lifecycle workflows require ID Governance**.

terms.d: Joiner, mover and leaver stages of an identity's existence.
ID Governance automation for joiner, mover and leaver tasks.
Creating accounts automatically from an HR system of record.
Standard protocol used to provision users into applications.

lessons.trap: Lifecycle workflows need an ID Governance licence (not just P2); recertifying existing access is an access review, not a lifecycle workflow.
lessons.example: Two days before a new nurse starts, a lifecycle workflow emails her manager a Temporary Access Pass; on her final day another workflow removes her group memberships and disables the account.

lessons.title: Entitlement management and terms of use
lessons.short: Entitlement management lets users request access through access packages: bundles of groups, Teams, applications and SharePoint sites with policies for who can request, who approves and when access expires. Resources are organized in catalogs, users request in the My Access portal, and users from connected organizations are onboarded as guests.
lessons.deep:
Handing out access one group at a time doesn't scale. **Entitlement management** automates access request workflows.
- **Catalog**: a container of resources (groups and Teams, apps, SharePoint Online sites) and access packages, which can be delegated to catalog owners.
- **Access package**: a bundle of resource roles a user needs for a project or job, requested as one unit.
- **Policy** on the package: **who can request** (internal users, specific connected organizations, any external user), **approval** (single or multi-stage, by managers, sponsors or named approvers), **expiration** of assignments, requestor justification and recurring **access reviews**.
- **Separation of duties**: mark packages as incompatible so one person can't hold both.
- **Connected organizations**: partner organizations whose users may request; approved users are added as **B2B guests** and automatically removed when their last assignment ends.
- Users browse and request in the **My Access portal** (myaccess.microsoft.com).

**Terms of use**: admins upload a PDF and enforce acceptance with the Conditional Access grant control **Require terms of use** before users reach an app.

terms.d: A requestable bundle of groups, apps and sites with policies.
Container holding resources and access packages, with delegated owners.
A partner organization whose users can request access packages.
End-user portal for requesting and viewing access packages.

lessons.trap: 'Bundle resources so people can request them with approval and automatic expiry' is entitlement management, not dynamic groups, access reviews or B2B direct connect.
lessons.example: For a six-month joint project, Fabrikam's engineers request a 'Project Falcon' access package; the project lead approves and the guests are removed automatically when it expires.

lessons.title: Access reviews
lessons.short: Access reviews let organizations regularly recertify who has access to groups, Microsoft 365 groups and Teams, enterprise applications, access packages and privileged roles. Reviewers (resource owners, managers, named people or the users themselves) approve or deny access, and results can be applied automatically to remove access that's no longer needed.
lessons.deep:
Access tends to pile up as people change jobs (**access creep**). **Access reviews** fight this by asking the right people, on a schedule, whether access is still needed.

What can be reviewed:
- **Group memberships** (security groups, Microsoft 365 groups and Teams), including guests.
- **Users assigned to enterprise applications**.
- **Access package assignments** (entitlement management).
- **Microsoft Entra roles and Azure resource roles** (configured through PIM).

**Reviewers**: group owners, specified users or groups, users' managers, or **self-review** (users attest their own access). Multi-stage reviews can chain reviewers.
