**Settings**: one-time or recurring (weekly through annually); duration; **recommendations** (for example flag users inactive recently); what to do if reviewers don't respond (no change, remove access, approve access, take recommendations); and **auto apply results to resource** so denied users are removed without manual work.

**Licensing**: P2 or Entra ID Governance; newer features such as inactive-user-only reviews and machine-learning-assisted reviews need ID Governance.

terms.d: Periodic attestation of whether existing access is still required.
Users confirm or give up their own access.
Automatically removes access that reviewers denied when the review ends.

lessons.trap: Access reviews recertify existing access; they don't grant new access (entitlement management) or activate roles (PIM).
lessons.example: Every quarter, owners of the 'Partners-Extranet' group review guest members; guests who are denied or haven't signed in are removed automatically.

lessons.title: Privileged Identity Management (PIM)
lessons.short: Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (PIM) reduces standing admin access. Users are made eligible for Microsoft Entra roles, Azure resource roles or group membership/ownership (PIM for Groups) and activate them just in time, for a limited period, with MFA, justification and optional approval. It needs Microsoft Entra ID P2 or ID Governance.
lessons.deep:
Permanent admin rights are a gift to attackers. **PIM** applies **just-in-time (JIT)** and **time-bound** access.

**Assignment types**:
- **Eligible**: the user must **activate** the role before using it.
- **Active**: the user has the permissions without doing anything.
Either type can be **permanent** or **time-bound** (start and end dates).

**Activation settings** (per role): maximum activation duration, **require MFA**, **require justification**, require ticket information, **require approval** from designated approvers, and Conditional Access authentication context.

**Oversight**:
- **Notifications** when roles are activated or assigned.
- **Access reviews** of role assignments.
- **Audit history** you can download for auditors.
- **Alerts**, for example too many Global Administrators or roles assigned outside PIM.
- Protection against removing the last Global Administrator.

**Scope**: Microsoft Entra roles, **Azure resource roles** (subscriptions, resource groups) and **PIM for Groups**. Licensing: **Entra ID P2 or Entra ID Governance**; the Privileged Role Administrator manages PIM.

terms.d: User can activate the role when needed but doesn't hold it standing.
User holds the role's permissions without activation.
Privileges granted only when needed and removed automatically.
JIT membership or ownership of groups through PIM.

lessons.trap: If the stem mentions standing admin access, activation on demand, approval for elevation or time-limited roles, the answer is PIM, not Conditional Access or entitlement management.
lessons.example: An engineer eligible for Exchange Administrator activates it for two hours, completes MFA, types the change ticket number, and loses the role automatically afterwards.

lessons.title: Microsoft Entra ID Protection: risk detections
lessons.short: Microsoft Entra ID Protection uses Microsoft threat intelligence and machine learning to detect identity risk. Sign-in risk is the probability a specific sign-in isn't from the account owner; user risk is the probability the account itself is compromised. Detections are real-time or offline and rated low, medium or high.
lessons.deep:
**ID Protection** analyses huge volumes of signals across Microsoft to spot compromised identities.

**Sign-in risk** (is *this sign-in* suspicious?) examples:
- **Anonymous IP address** (Tor or anonymizer VPN).
- **Atypical travel**: two sign-ins from locations too far apart to travel between in the time.
- **Unfamiliar sign-in properties**, **malicious IP address**, **password spray**.

**User risk** (is *the account* compromised?) examples:
- **Leaked credentials**: the user's username/password pair was found in a public or dark-web leak (needs PHS for synced users).
- **Anomalous user activity**, **Microsoft Entra threat intelligence**.
- **Admin confirmed user compromised**.

Detections are **real-time** (during sign-in) or **offline** (calculated afterwards), and each risk is **low, medium or high**. Risky sign-ins accumulate into user risk.

**Licensing**: full detections and risk-based policies need **P2**; Free/P1 tenants see limited information (premium detections show only as 'Additional risk detected'). Workload ID Premium adds risk detection for workload identities.

terms.d: Probability that a given authentication request isn't from the identity owner.
Probability that an identity or account is compromised.
User risk detection when credentials are found in a leak.
Risk calculated during the sign-in itself.

lessons.trap: Leaked credentials raise USER risk (the account is compromised), while anonymous IP and atypical travel raise SIGN-IN risk; swapping them is the classic distractor.
lessons.example: A user signs in from London and, 30 minutes later, from Singapore; ID Protection flags atypical travel and marks the second sign-in as medium risk.

lessons.title: ID Protection: risk policies, remediation and reports
lessons.short: ID Protection risk feeds Conditional Access: a sign-in risk policy typically requires MFA for medium or high risk, and a user risk policy requires a secure password change (or risk remediation) for high-risk users. Admins investigate in the risky users, risky sign-ins and risk detections reports. It requires Microsoft Entra ID P2.
lessons.deep:
Detection is only useful if something happens next. ID Protection risk is consumed by **risk-based Conditional Access policies** (P2):
- **Sign-in risk policy**: for example, if sign-in risk is medium or high, **require MFA**. Passing MFA proves it's the real user and closes the risky sign-in (**self-remediation**).
- **User risk policy**: for example, if user risk is high, **require a secure password change** or **require risk remediation**, which revokes sessions and, for password users, forces a secure password change.
- **MFA registration policy**: makes users register for MFA so they can self-remediate; users without registered MFA can't satisfy a risk policy and are blocked.

The legacy user risk and sign-in risk policies configured inside ID Protection have been retired; risk policies are now built as Conditional Access policies.

**Investigation reports**: **risky users**, **risky sign-ins**, **risk detections** (and risky workload identities). Admin actions include **confirm compromised**, **confirm safe**, **dismiss user risk**, reset password and block user. Feedback improves the model.

Risk data can be exported to Log Analytics or Microsoft Sentinel and appears in Microsoft Defender XDR.

terms.d: User clears their own risk by completing MFA or a secure password change.
Lists users at risk with their detection history.
Admin feedback that a detection was a false positive.
Requires users to register MFA so they can self-remediate.

lessons.trap: Sign-in risk maps to MFA; user risk maps to a secure password change. MFA alone does not remediate user risk.
lessons.example: A user whose credentials leaked is forced to change her password at next sign-in after MFA; her user risk drops to none without a helpdesk call.

lessons.title: Azure DDoS Protection
lessons.short: Azure DDoS Protection defends public-facing Azure resources against distributed denial-of-service floods. Every Azure public IP gets free infrastructure-level protection; the paid tiers, DDoS Network Protection and DDoS IP Protection, add tuned mitigation, telemetry and alerts.
lessons.deep:
A **denial-of-service (DoS)** attack tries to make a service unavailable by exhausting its bandwidth, connections or compute. In a **distributed** (DDoS) attack the traffic comes from thousands of compromised machines (a botnet), so blocking one source IP does not help.

Microsoft groups attacks into three categories:
- **Volumetric**: floods such as UDP or ICMP floods and reflection/amplification.
- **Protocol**: abuse of L3/L4 protocols, such as SYN floods or Ping of Death.
- **Resource (application) layer**: HTTP floods, Slowloris, SQL injection, XSS.

Azure DDoS Protection mitigates the **L3/L4** volumetric and protocol attacks automatically, using always-on traffic monitoring and the scale of Microsoft's global network. For **layer 7** attacks Microsoft says to add a **web application firewall (WAF)**.

Tiers:
- **Infrastructure protection**: free, automatic for all Azure services with public IPs, no configuration, but no tuning, metrics or alerts for you.
- **DDoS IP Protection**: billed per protected public IP; tuned mitigation, metrics, alerts, mitigation reports, Sentinel integration.
- **DDoS Network Protection**: enabled by associating a **DDoS protection plan** with virtual networks; adds **DDoS Rapid Response** (DRR) team support, **cost protection** (credits for scale-out costs caused by an attack) and a **WAF discount**.

terms.d: Distributed denial of service: many sources flood a target to make it unavailable.
Paid tier applied via a DDoS protection plan on VNets; includes rapid response, cost protection and WAF discount.
Paid tier billed per public IP; core mitigation and telemetry without rapid response or cost protection.
Flood of traffic that saturates bandwidth, e.g. UDP flood.

lessons.trap: Exams offer DDoS IP Protection when the scenario needs Rapid Response or cost protection; only DDoS Network Protection includes those.
lessons.example: An online retailer links a DDoS protection plan to its production VNet before Black Friday so it gets Rapid Response support and cost protection if attacked.

lessons.title: Azure Firewall
lessons.short: Azure Firewall is a managed, cloud-native, stateful firewall service with built-in high availability and autoscaling. It centrally filters inbound, outbound and east-west traffic using NAT, network and application (FQDN) rules, plus threat intelligence filtering.
lessons.deep:
**Azure Firewall** is a firewall-as-a-service: Microsoft runs, patches and scales it, you write the rules. It is usually placed in a **hub virtual network** in a **hub-and-spoke** design, with **user-defined routes** sending spoke traffic through it, so one policy governs traffic between spokes, to the internet and from on-premises.

Rule types:
- **DNAT rules**: translate inbound traffic on the firewall's public IP to a private IP and port.
- **Network rules**: allow/deny by source, destination, port and protocol (L3/L4).
- **Application rules**: allow/deny outbound HTTP/HTTPS/SQL by **FQDN**, including wildcards and FQDN tags.

**Threat intelligence-based filtering** uses Microsoft Threat Intelligence to alert on or deny traffic to known malicious IPs and domains. Logs go to Azure Monitor and Microsoft Sentinel. **Azure Firewall Manager** and **firewall policies** let you manage many firewalls centrally.

SKUs:
- **Basic**: small businesses, up to 250 Mbps, threat intel alert-only.
- **Standard**: up to 30 Gbps, threat intel deny, web categories, DNS proxy.
- **Premium**: adds **TLS inspection**, signature-based **IDPS** and full-path **URL filtering** for sensitive workloads such as payments.

Compare with NSGs: an NSG is a free, distributed L3/L4 filter on a subnet or NIC; Azure Firewall is a central, paid service that understands FQDNs and applications.

terms.d: Tracks connections so return traffic for an allowed flow is allowed automatically.
Azure Firewall rule filtering outbound web traffic by fully qualified domain name.
Intrusion detection and prevention system; signature-based, in Azure Firewall Premium.
Topology where shared services like the firewall sit in a hub VNet peered to workload spokes.

lessons.trap: Questions that need FQDN filtering or central logging across VNets want Azure Firewall, not an NSG; TLS inspection and IDPS mean Premium specifically.
lessons.example: A bank routes all spoke VNet traffic through Azure Firewall Premium in its hub so it can inspect TLS traffic and allow outbound access only to approved partner domains.

lessons.title: Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF)
lessons.short: Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF) centrally protects web applications from common exploits such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting. You deploy it on Azure Application Gateway, Azure Front Door, Application Gateway for Containers or Azure CDN, using managed rule sets and custom rules.
lessons.deep:
Web apps are attacked at **layer 7** (HTTP/HTTPS) with techniques from the **OWASP Top 10**: SQL injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), protocol violations and more. Fixing every app individually is slow, so **Azure WAF** puts a shared, centrally managed shield in front of them.

Where it runs:
- **Azure Application Gateway**: regional layer-7 load balancer; WAF protects apps in that region.
- **Azure Front Door**: global edge service; WAF blocks attacks at Microsoft's edge before they reach your origin.
- **Application Gateway for Containers** and **Azure CDN** (CDN integration is in preview).

How it works:
- **Managed rule sets**: Microsoft's **Default Rule Set (DRS)** or the **OWASP Core Rule Set (CRS)**, updated by Microsoft.
- **Bot protection**: Bot Manager rule set separates good, bad and unknown bots.
- **Custom rules**: evaluated before managed rules; match on IP, geo-location (**geo-match**), headers, rate limits, then ALLOW, BLOCK or LOG.
- **Modes**: **Detection** logs matches without blocking; **Prevention** blocks matches (Application Gateway returns 403). Microsoft suggests starting in Detection to tune false positives.

WAF complements, not replaces, DDoS Protection (L3/L4) and Azure Firewall (network traffic).

terms.d: Container for WAF settings: mode, managed rule sets, exclusions and custom rules.
Open Worldwide Application Security Project; its Top 10 lists the most critical web risks.
WAF mode that blocks requests matching rules.
WAF mode that only logs matching requests.

lessons.trap: WAF is the answer for SQL injection/XSS; the exam uses Azure Firewall or NSGs as distractors, which do not inspect web request content this way.
lessons.example: A travel site puts WAF on Azure Front Door so SQL injection attempts and traffic from blocked countries are dropped at the edge before reaching its App Service origin.

lessons.title: Network segmentation with Azure virtual networks
lessons.short: An Azure virtual network (VNet) is a private, isolated network in one region, divided into subnets. Segmenting workloads into separate VNets and subnets, then allowing only required flows, limits lateral movement and supports Zero Trust's assume-breach principle.
lessons.deep:
**Segmentation** means splitting a network into smaller zones so a compromise in one zone cannot spread freely. Azure gives you the building blocks:

- **Virtual network (VNet)**: a logically isolated private address space (e.g. 10.0.0.0/16) scoped to **one region** and subscription. Resources in different VNets **cannot talk to each other by default**.
- **Subnets**: ranges inside a VNet. By default, subnets in the same VNet can reach each other; you restrict that with **NSGs**.
- **VNet peering**: connects VNets privately over Microsoft's backbone. Peering is **not transitive**: if A peers with B and B with C, A cannot reach C unless you peer them or route through a hub.
- **User-defined routes (UDRs)/route tables**: override default routing, e.g. force spoke traffic through Azure Firewall in the hub.
- **Private endpoints**: give a PaaS service (Storage, SQL) a private IP in your VNet so traffic never needs its public endpoint.
- **VPN Gateway / ExpressRoute**: extend the network to on-premises.

A typical design is **hub-and-spoke**: shared security services (Azure Firewall, Bastion) in the hub, workloads in isolated spokes. Within an app, separate **web, app and data tiers** into subnets so the database accepts traffic only from the app tier.

terms.d: Isolated private network in Azure, scoped to one region.
Private, non-transitive connection between two VNets.
Custom route in a route table that overrides Azure's default routing.
Network interface with a private IP that connects a VNet to a PaaS resource.

lessons.trap: Exams test that VNets are isolated by default and peering is non-transitive; 'NSG' is a wrong answer when the question is how to connect two VNets.
lessons.example: A hospital puts its patient-records database in a dedicated subnet whose NSG allows SQL traffic only from the application subnet, so a compromised web server cannot reach it directly.

lessons.title: Network security groups (NSGs)
lessons.short: A network security group (NSG) is a free, stateful filter of allow and deny rules for inbound and outbound traffic, associated with a subnet or a network interface. Rules are processed by priority (100-4096, lowest number first) and stop at the first match.
lessons.deep:
An **NSG** holds **security rules** evaluated on the five-tuple: source, source port, destination, destination port, protocol. Each rule has a **name**, **priority**, **source/destination** (IP, CIDR, **service tag** or **application security group**), **protocol** (TCP, UDP, ICMP, Any…), **direction**, **port range** and **action** (Allow/Deny).

**Priority**: 100 to 4096; lower numbers are processed first, and processing **stops at the first matching rule**.

**Default rules** (priority 65000+, cannot be deleted, can be overridden by your rules):
- Inbound: AllowVNetInBound (65000), AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound (65001), **DenyAllInbound** (65500).
- Outbound: AllowVnetOutBound (65000), **AllowInternetOutBound** (65001), DenyAllOutBound (65500).

NSGs are **stateful**: if outbound traffic is allowed, the response is allowed back automatically.

**Association**: to a **subnet** and/or a **NIC**. For inbound traffic the subnet NSG is evaluated first, then the NIC NSG; outbound is the reverse. Traffic must be allowed by both.

**Service tags** (e.g. `Internet`, `VirtualNetwork`, `AzureLoadBalancer`, `Storage`) are Microsoft-maintained IP groups. **Application security groups (ASGs)** group VMs by role (e.g. web servers) so rules don't depend on IPs.

terms.d: Number 100-4096; lower is evaluated first, first match wins.
Named, Microsoft-maintained group of IP prefixes for an Azure service.
Logical group of VM NICs used as an NSG rule source or destination.
Default rule (65500) that blocks inbound traffic not allowed by a higher-priority rule.

lessons.trap: Candidates think Allow beats Deny; in an NSG the rule with the lowest priority number that matches wins, whatever its action.
lessons.example: An admin adds an inbound rule at priority 110 allowing TCP 443 from the Internet service tag to an ASG called web-servers; everything else still hits DenyAllInbound.

lessons.title: Azure Bastion
lessons.short: Azure Bastion is a fully managed PaaS service that gives secure RDP and SSH access to VMs over TLS from the Azure portal, so VMs need no public IP and RDP/SSH ports are never exposed to the internet.
lessons.deep:
Opening RDP (3389) or SSH (22) to the internet invites port scanning and brute-force attacks. **Azure Bastion** removes that exposure:

1. You deploy Bastion into a dedicated subnet named **AzureBastionSubnet** (size **/26 or larger**) in the VNet.
2. An admin signs in to the Azure portal and chooses **Connect > Bastion** on a VM.
3. The browser session runs over **TLS on port 443** to Bastion.
4. Bastion opens RDP/SSH to the VM's **private IP** inside the VNet.

Benefits: no **public IP** on VMs, no client or agent required for browser sessions, Microsoft hardens and patches the Bastion host, and NSGs can block RDP/SSH from everywhere except Bastion. Bastion can reach VMs in **peered VNets** (except the Developer SKU).

SKUs:
- **Developer**: free, shared, one connection at a time, same VNet only, no AzureBastionSubnet needed; not for production.
- **Basic**: dedicated hosts, browser RDP/SSH.
- **Standard**: adds **native client** support (Azure CLI), **shareable links**, **IP-based connection**, custom ports, file transfer.
- **Premium**: adds **session recording** and **private-only** deployment (no public IP on Bastion).

terms.d: Required subnet name for Bastion Basic/Standard/Premium; /26 or larger.
Hardened host used to reach other servers; Bastion is a managed one.
Bastion Premium feature that records RDP/SSH sessions for audit.

lessons.trap: Just-in-time VM access is the classic distractor: JIT only opens ports temporarily, whereas Bastion means the VM needs no public IP at all.
lessons.example: An MSP removes public IPs from 40 VMs and gives engineers Azure Bastion Standard so they can connect with their native SSH client through the Azure CLI.

lessons.title: Azure Key Vault
lessons.short: Azure Key Vault is a cloud service for securely storing and controlling access to secrets, cryptographic keys and TLS/SSL certificates. Access is authenticated by Microsoft Entra ID and authorized with Azure RBAC or access policies, and every access can be logged.
lessons.deep:
Hard-coding passwords or connection strings in code or config files leaks them through source control. **Azure Key Vault** centralizes three object types:
- **Secrets**: passwords, API keys, connection strings.
- **Keys**: cryptographic keys for encryption and signing (e.g. customer-managed keys for Storage).
- **Certificates**: TLS/SSL certificates, including lifecycle and renewal.

**Access**: authentication always uses **Microsoft Entra ID**. Authorization uses **Azure RBAC** (Microsoft's recommended model; covers management and data) or legacy **access policies** (data plane only). Built-in roles include **Key Vault Administrator**, **Key Vault Secrets Officer**, **Key Vault Secrets User** (read secret values) and **Key Vault Reader** (metadata only, not secret values). Apps use a **managed identity** so there's no credential to store at all.

**Tiers**: **Standard** uses software-protected keys (FIPS 140 Level 1); **Premium** adds **HSM-protected keys** (FIPS 140-3 Level 3). **Managed HSM** is a separate single-tenant offering.

**Recovery**: **soft-delete** is on by default and cannot be turned off; deleted items are retained 7-90 days (default **90**, set at creation). **Purge protection** is optional; when on, nobody can permanently purge a deleted item until retention ends.

**Monitoring**: diagnostic logs to Azure Monitor, storage or Event Hubs.

terms.d: Small sensitive value such as a password or connection string.
Hardware security module: tamper-resistant device that generates and holds keys.
Keeps deleted vaults and objects recoverable for 7-90 days.
Prevents permanent deletion until the retention period ends.

lessons.trap: Key Vault Reader sounds right for reading secrets but only reads metadata; reading a secret's value needs Key Vault Secrets User.
lessons.example: A web app's managed identity is granted Key Vault Secrets User, so the app fetches its database password at startup and no password appears in its configuration.

lessons.title: Microsoft Defender for Cloud overview
lessons.short: Microsoft Defender for Cloud is a cloud-native application protection platform (CNAPP) that secures Azure, hybrid and multicloud resources. It combines DevSecOps, cloud security posture management (CSPM) and cloud workload protection (CWPP) in one service.
lessons.deep:
Securing cloud resources involves two different questions: **is it configured safely?** and **is it being attacked right now?** Microsoft Defender for Cloud answers both, plus a third: **is the code that deploys it safe?** That combination is called a **CNAPP**.

The three pillars:
- **DevSecOps**: connects code repositories (Azure DevOps, GitHub, GitLab) and surfaces issues like infrastructure-as-code misconfigurations and exposed secrets, from code to cloud.
- **CSPM**: continuously assesses resource configurations against security standards, produces **recommendations** and a **secure score**. **Foundational CSPM** is free; **Defender CSPM** is a paid plan with advanced features.
- **CWPP**: paid **Defender plans** (Servers, Storage, Databases, Containers, App Service, Key Vault, Resource Manager, APIs, AI services) detect threats and raise **security alerts**.

Alerts and incidents can be exported to a **SIEM/SOAR** such as **Microsoft Sentinel**, or ITSM tools. Many Defender for Cloud experiences also appear in the **Microsoft Defender portal**, alongside Defender XDR.

A simple way to remember it: **assess** (posture), **secure** (harden using recommendations), **defend** (detect and respond with workload protection).

terms.d: Cloud-native application protection platform: posture, workload protection and DevSecOps together.
Cloud security posture management: finding and fixing misconfigurations.
Cloud workload protection platform: threat detection for running workloads.

lessons.trap: Defender for Cloud is a CNAPP, not a SIEM; when the question is about collecting logs from everything and hunting, the answer is Microsoft Sentinel.
lessons.example: A SaaS start-up uses free Foundational CSPM to harden its Azure subscriptions, then enables Defender for Servers and Defender for Storage on production workloads.

lessons.title: Multicloud, hybrid and DevOps coverage
lessons.short: Defender for Cloud is not Azure-only. Connectors bring AWS accounts and GCP projects under the same posture and protection, Azure Arc onboards on-premises and other-cloud servers, and DevOps security connects Azure DevOps, GitHub and GitLab repositories.
lessons.deep:
Most organizations run more than one environment, so one console for posture matters.

- **AWS and GCP**: you add a **connector** for an AWS account or GCP project. Defender for Cloud uses **agentless** methods to read configuration, assesses it against standards (including MCSB and cloud-provider benchmarks), and shows recommendations and secure score alongside Azure. Paid plans such as Defender for Servers and Defender for Containers can protect workloads there too.
- **On-premises and hybrid**: Microsoft recommends onboarding non-Azure machines as **Azure Arc-enabled servers** so they get the full set of Defender for Servers features. Arc gives the machine an Azure resource identity so policies and recommendations apply.
- **DevOps security**: connect **Azure DevOps**, **GitHub** or **GitLab** to see code and pipeline findings: IaC template misconfigurations, secrets in code, and open-source dependency vulnerabilities. Defender CSPM can then map a cloud resource back to the code that deployed it (**code-to-cloud**).

Result: security teams see Azure, AWS, GCP, on-premises and code risks in one prioritized list instead of three separate consoles.

terms.d: Defender for Cloud link to an AWS account or GCP project.
Projects non-Azure servers and clusters into Azure Resource Manager for management.
Templates such as Bicep or Terraform that define cloud resources.

lessons.trap: A common wrong answer says Defender for Cloud protects only Azure; it covers AWS, GCP and on-premises (via Azure Arc) too.
lessons.example: A retailer connects three AWS accounts and its GitHub organization to Defender for Cloud and finds an S3 bucket and a Terraform template both allowing public access.

lessons.title: Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM)
lessons.short: CSPM continuously finds misconfigurations and weaknesses in cloud resources and tells you how to fix them. Defender for Cloud offers free Foundational CSPM (secure score, MCSB recommendations) and the paid Defender CSPM plan with attack path analysis, cloud security explorer and more.
lessons.deep:
**Posture** is how well your environment is configured: open management ports, missing MFA, unencrypted storage, unpatched VMs. Most cloud breaches start from such misconfigurations, not exotic exploits. **CSPM** is the discipline of continuously spotting and fixing them.

**Foundational CSPM (free)**:
- Continuous assessment against the **Microsoft cloud security benchmark (MCSB)**.
- **Security recommendations** with remediation steps.
- **Secure score**.
- Asset inventory and DevOps code findings.

**Defender CSPM (paid)** adds:
- **Attack path analysis**: shows chains an attacker could follow, e.g. internet-exposed VM with a vulnerability that has a path to a storage account holding sensitive data.
- **Risk hunting with cloud security explorer**: graph queries across resources.
- **Agentless scanning** of VMs for vulnerabilities and secrets, and agentless container/Kubernetes discovery.
- **Governance** rules to assign owners and due dates at scale.
- **Data security posture management**: sensitive data discovery.
- **Regulatory compliance assessments** and **AI security posture management**.

CSPM is about **prevention**: fixing weaknesses before they are exploited. Detecting active attacks is the job of CWPP plans.

terms.d: Free Defender for Cloud tier: MCSB assessment, recommendations, secure score.
Paid plan adding attack paths, security explorer, agentless scanning, governance.
Graph showing how exploitable weaknesses chain toward critical assets.

lessons.trap: Exams list secure score and attack path analysis side by side; secure score is free, attack path analysis needs Defender CSPM.
lessons.example: Defender CSPM shows an attack path from an internet-facing VM with a critical CVE to a storage account with credit-card data, so the team patches that VM first.

lessons.title: Security policies, standards and recommendations
lessons.short: In Defender for Cloud a security policy contains security standards; each standard holds controls with assessment logic. When a resource fails a control, Defender for Cloud generates a security recommendation with remediation steps. The Microsoft cloud security benchmark (MCSB) is applied by default.
lessons.deep:
The chain from rulebook to action:

1. **Security standards** define what 'good' looks like. Three kinds:
   - **Security benchmarks**: the **Microsoft cloud security benchmark (MCSB)**, applied by default when you enable Defender for Cloud, plus cloud-provider benchmarks.
   - **Regulatory compliance standards**: e.g. ISO 27001, PCI DSS, NIST SP 800-53; you can add these once a paid Defender plan is enabled (any plan except Defender for Servers Plan 1 or Defender for APIs Plan 1), and track them on the **regulatory compliance dashboard**.
   - **Custom standards**: your own selection of built-in or custom recommendations (custom KQL-based recommendations need Defender CSPM).
2. A **security policy** groups the standards assigned to a scope (subscription, AWS account, GCP project). In Azure, standards are implemented using **Azure Policy**.
3. Defender for Cloud continuously **assesses** resources against each control.
4. A resource that fails becomes **unhealthy/noncompliant**, and a **recommendation** is created: issue description, remediation steps, affected resources, severity and risk factors.
5. You remediate manually, use **Fix** (quick fix), or use **Enforce/Deny** so new noncompliant resources can't be created. **Exemptions** handle accepted exceptions.

Risk prioritization ranks recommendations by exposure, data sensitivity and exploitability, but does not change the secure score.

terms.d: Set of controls and assessment logic, e.g. MCSB or PCI DSS.
Microsoft cloud security benchmark: Microsoft's default multicloud security baseline.
Actionable finding with remediation steps for a failed control.
Options that stop new noncompliant resources from being deployed.

lessons.trap: Recommendations are posture findings about configuration; security alerts are threat detections. Exams swap the two.
lessons.example: MCSB requires storage accounts to restrict network access; a storage account open to all networks is flagged unhealthy and a recommendation tells the admin to add network rules.

lessons.title: Secure score
lessons.short: Secure score turns Defender for Cloud's posture findings into a single number: higher means lower identified risk. In the classic model, points are grouped into security controls, and you earn a control's points only when all its recommendations are fixed for all resources.
lessons.deep:
**Secure score** gives leaders and engineers one metric to track posture over time.

**Classic secure score** (Azure portal, shown as a percentage):
- Recommendations are grouped into **security controls** such as *Enable MFA* (max 10 points), *Secure management ports* (8), *Apply system updates* (6), *Remediate vulnerabilities* (6).
- Each control's **max score** reflects its importance. Points are earned in proportion to healthy resources, but the control's full points come only when **all** its recommendations are remediated on **all** resources.
- Only built-in **MCSB** recommendations count; **preview** recommendations don't count until generally available.
- The **potential score increase** shown on each control tells you which fixes raise the score most.

**Cloud Secure Score** (Microsoft Defender portal, 0-100) is **risk-based**: it weighs open recommendations by risk level, asset risk factors (e.g. internet exposure, sensitive data) and **asset criticality**.

You can view the score per subscription or management group, query it with **Azure Resource Graph**, track it over time with workbooks or Power BI, or retrieve it through the Secure Scores REST API.

terms.d: Group of related recommendations with a maximum point value.
Points you would gain by fixing a control's unhealthy resources.
Risk-based 0-100 score in the Defender portal weighting asset criticality.

lessons.trap: Fixing one recommendation in a control does not earn that control's full points; all recommendations for all resources must be healthy.
lessons.example: A CISO sees 'Enable MFA' offers the largest potential score increase, so the team enforces MFA on all subscription owners first.

lessons.title: Cloud workload protection: Defender plans
lessons.short: Enhanced security features are the paid Defender plans that add cloud workload protection (CWPP) on top of free posture management. Each plan targets a resource type, such as servers, storage, databases, containers or Key Vault, and raises security alerts when it detects threats.
lessons.deep:
Posture management reduces weaknesses, but attackers still try. **Cloud workload protection** watches running resources and alerts on suspicious behaviour. In Defender for Cloud you turn it on by enabling **Defender plans** (often called **enhanced security features**), usually per subscription.

Key plans:
- **Defender for Servers** (Plan 1 / Plan 2): Windows and Linux machines in Azure, AWS, GCP and on-premises.
- **Defender for Storage**: malware scanning of uploads, sensitive data threat detection, suspicious access such as SAS token misuse.
- **Defender for Databases**: Azure SQL, SQL on machines, open-source relational databases, Azure Cosmos DB.
- **Defender for Containers**: Kubernetes hardening, image vulnerability assessment, runtime threat detection.
- **Defender for App Service**, **Defender for Key Vault** (unusual vault access), **Defender for Resource Manager** (suspicious management operations), **Defender for APIs**, and **AI threat protection** for generative AI workloads.

**Security alerts** describe the threat, affected resource, MITRE ATT&CK tactics and remediation steps; related alerts are correlated into **incidents**. Alerts can be streamed to Microsoft Sentinel or other SIEMs, and appear in the Microsoft Defender portal.

terms.d: The paid Defender plans in Defender for Cloud.
Notification of a detected threat on a protected resource.
Plan that detects suspicious Azure management-layer operations.

lessons.trap: Free Foundational CSPM gives recommendations but no threat-detection alerts; alerts require a paid Defender plan.
lessons.example: After enabling Defender for Storage, a company is alerted when a malicious file is uploaded to a blob container used by its customer portal.

lessons.title: Defender for Servers and just-in-time VM access
lessons.short: Defender for Servers protects Windows and Linux machines. Plan 1 provides Microsoft Defender for Endpoint EDR integration; Plan 2 adds agentless scanning, premium Defender Vulnerability Management, file integrity monitoring, just-in-time VM access and more.
lessons.deep:
**Defender for Servers** is the most-used workload plan.

**Plan 1**: integrates **Microsoft Defender for Endpoint** for endpoint detection and response (**EDR**) on servers. Can be enabled per subscription or for individual resources.

**Plan 2**: everything in Plan 1 plus:
- **Agentless scanning** for vulnerabilities, malware, secrets and posture.
- **Premium Defender Vulnerability Management** features.
- **File integrity monitoring (FIM)**: detects changes to critical OS files and registry.
- **Just-in-time (JIT) VM access**.
- OS configuration and update assessment, network map, a free data ingestion benefit for certain data types, and suspicious DNS activity alerts.

**How JIT works**: management ports (RDP 3389, SSH 22) are locked with deny rules in the **NSG** (and Azure Firewall). A user requests access; Defender for Cloud checks their **Azure RBAC** permissions; if approved, it opens the port **only for the requester's IP and only for the approved time**, then restores the rules. Established connections aren't cut.

For on-premises and other-cloud machines, onboard via **Azure Arc** for the full feature set.

terms.d: Endpoint detection and response: records endpoint activity and detects/responds to attacks.
Opens management ports only on request, for a limited time and source IP.
Tracks changes to important files and registry keys.

lessons.trap: JIT and FIM are Plan 2 features; a question asking for EDR at the lowest cost points to Plan 1.
lessons.example: An admin requests three hours of RDP access to a VM; Defender for Cloud opens 3389 only from her office IP and closes it automatically afterwards.

lessons.title: SIEM and SOAR concepts
lessons.short: A SIEM (security information and event management) collects, stores and correlates security data from many sources to detect threats. SOAR (security orchestration, automation and response) uses playbooks to automate and coordinate the response. Microsoft Sentinel is a cloud-native SIEM and SOAR.
lessons.deep:
A security operations centre (SOC) gets logs from firewalls, servers, identity systems, SaaS apps and endpoints. Looking at each console separately is slow, so organisations centralise.

**SIEM** = security information and event management. It:
- **collects** logs and events from many sources
- **normalises** them so different formats can be compared
- **correlates** events with detection rules to raise **alerts**
- groups related alerts into **incidents** and gives dashboards and long-term search for investigations and compliance

**SOAR** = security orchestration, automation and response. It takes the output of the SIEM and acts on it:
- **orchestration**: connects many tools (ticketing, firewall, identity, email)
- **automation**: runs repeatable steps without a human, using **playbooks**
- **response**: contains threats fast, e.g. disable an account or block an IP

Together they shorten the time to detect and the time to respond. **Microsoft Sentinel** provides both in one cloud-native service, so there is no SIEM hardware to buy or scale. Compare with **XDR** (Microsoft Defender XDR), which focuses on protecting and correlating Microsoft's own security products; a SIEM can ingest data from almost anything.

terms.d: Security information and event management: collects and correlates log data to detect threats.
Security orchestration, automation and response: automates response steps across tools with playbooks.
A predefined, automated set of response actions run when an alert or incident occurs.
A group of related alerts that together tell the story of one attack.

lessons.trap: Exams swap the two: detection/correlation of logs is SIEM, automated response with playbooks is SOAR; Sentinel does both.
lessons.example: Sentinel correlates failed sign-ins from Entra ID with a firewall alert (SIEM), then a playbook disables the account and opens a ServiceNow ticket (SOAR).

lessons.title: Microsoft Sentinel: collect and detect
lessons.short: Microsoft Sentinel collects data with data connectors into a Log Analytics workspace, then detects threats with analytics rules, threat intelligence, watchlists and UEBA. Workbooks give interactive visual reports of the data.
lessons.deep:
Sentinel's work can be remembered as **collect, detect, investigate, respond**. This lesson covers the first two.

**Collect**
- **Data connectors** bring in data from Microsoft sources (Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft 365, Defender XDR, Azure Activity), other clouds, and third-party products. Generic methods include **Syslog**, **Common Event Format (CEF)** and REST APIs, and you can build custom connectors.
- Data lands in a **Log Analytics workspace** and is queried with **KQL** (Kusto Query Language).
- **ASIM** (Advanced Security Information Model) normalises different sources into a common schema.

**Detect**
- **Analytics rules** search the data and raise alerts and incidents. Types include **scheduled** query rules (run a KQL query on an interval), **near-real-time (NRT)** rules (run about every minute), **anomaly** rules that use machine learning, and **threat intelligence** matching rules.
- **Threat intelligence** indicators (IPs, domains, URLs, file hashes) are matched against your logs.
- **Watchlists** let you correlate your own lists, such as VIP users or terminated employees.
- **UEBA** (user and entity behaviour analytics) builds baselines and flags unusual behaviour.
- **Workbooks** are interactive dashboards built on Azure Monitor workbooks, with many templates.
- A **MITRE ATT&CK** view shows your detection coverage.

terms.d: Built-in or custom integration that ingests data from a source into Sentinel.
Detection logic (often a KQL query) that raises alerts and creates incidents.
Interactive dashboard/report for visualising and monitoring Sentinel data.
Your own list of data (e.g. VIP users) used to enrich and correlate detections.
Kusto Query Language, used to query Log Analytics, Sentinel and advanced hunting.

lessons.trap: Workbooks visualise data, analytics rules detect, data connectors ingest; the exam offers all three as options for each other's job.
lessons.example: A company connects Entra ID sign-in logs and its Palo Alto firewall via CEF, enables a scheduled rule for impossible travel, and builds a workbook of failed sign-ins by country.

lessons.title: Microsoft Sentinel: investigate, hunt and respond
lessons.short: Sentinel incidents show related alerts, entities and an investigation graph. Analysts hunt proactively with KQL queries and Jupyter notebooks. Automation rules and playbooks built on Azure Logic Apps automate the response. Sentinel is moving fully into the Microsoft Defender portal.
lessons.deep:
**Investigate**
- **Incidents** group related alerts and their **entities** (users, hosts, IPs, files). An interactive investigation graph and timeline help find scope and root cause.
- **Threat hunting** is proactive: analysts search for attackers before any alert fires, using built-in **hunting queries** mapped to MITRE ATT&CK, **livestream**, and **bookmarks** to save findings. A useful hunting query can be turned into an analytics rule.
- **Notebooks** are **Jupyter notebooks** (running in Azure Machine Learning) for advanced analysis, machine learning and external data.

**Respond (SOAR)**
- **Automation rules** are lightweight rules that run when incidents or alerts are created or updated: assign an owner, change severity, add tags, close noise, or **run a playbook**.
- **Playbooks** are workflows built on **Azure Logic Apps**, with hundreds of connectors (Microsoft Teams, ServiceNow, Jira, Entra ID) to, for example, block a user, isolate a device or notify the SOC.

**Where Sentinel lives**: Sentinel is generally available in the **Microsoft Defender portal**, alongside Defender XDR, giving one incident queue and unified advanced hunting. Microsoft has announced that Sentinel in the Azure portal is supported only until **31 March 2027**, after which it is available only in the Defender portal.

terms.d: Proactively searching data for hidden threats before an alert is raised.
Rule that runs on incident/alert creation or update to triage or trigger playbooks.
Workflow service that Sentinel playbooks are built on.
Jupyter notebook for advanced, code-based investigation and analysis.

lessons.trap: Playbooks are built on Azure Logic Apps (not Azure Functions or Automation runbooks), and hunting does not need an alert first.
lessons.example: An automation rule sees a high-severity incident involving a VIP watchlist user, assigns it to tier-2 and runs a Logic Apps playbook that posts to Teams and revokes the user's sessions.

lessons.title: Microsoft Defender XDR and its services
lessons.short: Microsoft Defender XDR is a unified pre- and post-breach enterprise defence suite. It natively coordinates detection, prevention, investigation and response across endpoints, identities, email and collaboration, and cloud apps, correlating signals into incidents in the Microsoft Defender portal.
lessons.deep:
**XDR** means extended detection and response: instead of each product alerting on its own, signals from several domains are combined.

**Core services in Microsoft Defender XDR**
- **Microsoft Defender for Endpoint**: devices (Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS)
- **Microsoft Defender for Office 365**: email and collaboration (Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive)
- **Microsoft Defender for Identity**: on-premises Active Directory and hybrid identity
- **Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps**: SaaS apps (CASB)
- **Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management**: vulnerabilities and misconfigurations

It also integrates **Microsoft Entra ID Protection** (risky users and sign-ins), **Microsoft Purview** DLP and insider risk alerts, Microsoft Defender for Cloud alerts, and **Microsoft Sentinel**.

**Why it matters**: a real attack crosses domains, e.g. phishing email, then malware on a laptop, then stolen credentials used against a domain controller. Defender XDR stitches those alerts into **one incident**, shows the full attack story, and can respond across products (quarantine email, isolate device, disable user).

**XDR vs SIEM**: XDR is deep, native protection for Microsoft workloads; a SIEM such as Sentinel ingests data from almost any source. Microsoft combines them in the Defender portal for unified security operations.

terms.d: Extended detection and response: correlates signals across multiple security domains.
Microsoft's unified suite across endpoint, identity, email and cloud apps.
Preventing compromise vs. detecting and responding after it happens.

lessons.trap: Defender XDR covers Microsoft workloads natively; when the scenario needs logs from third-party firewalls or other clouds in one place, the answer is Microsoft Sentinel.
lessons.example: A user opens a phishing attachment; Defender XDR links the Defender for Office 365 email alert, the Defender for Endpoint malware alert and a Defender for Identity reconnaissance alert into one incident.

lessons.title: Defender XDR incidents, automation and advanced hunting
lessons.short: Defender XDR correlates alerts into incidents, runs automated investigation and response (AIR), and uses automatic attack disruption to contain in-progress attacks such as ransomware. Advanced hunting lets analysts query up to 30 days of raw data with KQL.
lessons.deep:
**Incidents and alerts**: an **alert** is one detection; an **incident** is the correlated collection of alerts, devices, users, mailboxes and evidence for one attack. Analysts manage one incident queue instead of many product queues.

**Automated investigation and response (AIR)**: when an alert fires, Defender XDR can automatically investigate the entities, decide whether evidence is malicious, and remediate (for example quarantine a file or soft-delete an email). Actions are approved or reviewed in the **Action center**, which lists pending and completed remediation actions.

**Automatic attack disruption**: for high-confidence, in-progress attacks such as human-operated ransomware, business email compromise or adversary-in-the-middle, Defender XDR automatically contains attacker-controlled assets, e.g. **contain device** (Defender for Endpoint) or **disable user** (Defender for Identity / Entra ID). It buys the SOC time; the team stays in control and **all automatic actions can be undone**. Critical assets can be excluded.

**Advanced hunting**: a query-based tool using **KQL** over tables such as `DeviceProcessEvents`, `EmailEvents`, `IdentityLogonEvents` and `CloudAppEvents`. You can explore raw data (default 30 days in the Defender XDR tables), build **custom detection rules** from queries, and, with Sentinel connected, query Sentinel data in the same place.

terms.d: Automated containment of compromised users/devices during a high-confidence attack.
Automated investigation and response: auto-investigates alerts and remediates threats.
Defender portal page listing pending and completed remediation actions.
KQL-based threat hunting over raw Defender XDR (and Sentinel) data.

lessons.trap: Attack disruption actions are reversible by the SOC; the exam may claim they are permanent or that they replace analysts.
lessons.example: Ransomware starts encrypting a file server; attack disruption disables the compromised admin account and contains the source device within minutes, then the analyst investigates and releases the device.

lessons.title: Defender for Office 365: EOP and Plan 1
lessons.short: Exchange Online Protection (EOP) gives every cloud mailbox anti-malware, anti-spam and basic anti-spoofing. Defender for Office 365 Plan 1 adds Safe Attachments, Safe Links, and impersonation protection in anti-phishing policies, covering email, Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive.
lessons.deep:
**Exchange Online Protection (EOP)** is built into all Microsoft 365 cloud mailboxes:
- anti-malware, anti-spam (including bulk mail), outbound spam protection
- anti-phishing with **spoof intelligence**
- connection filtering, quarantine, Tenant Allow/Block List
- **zero-hour auto purge (ZAP)**: removes malicious mail already delivered
- message trace and email reports

**Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Plan 1** adds protection against zero-day and targeted threats:
- **Safe Attachments**: opens unknown attachments in a virtual environment (detonation/sandbox) before delivery to see if they behave maliciously; also scans files in **SharePoint, OneDrive and Microsoft Teams**
- **Safe Links**: rewrites URLs and checks them **at time of click** in email, Office apps and Teams, so a link that becomes malicious after delivery is still blocked
- **Anti-phishing impersonation protection**: user impersonation (e.g. a fake CEO), domain impersonation (lookalike domains), and **mailbox intelligence** that learns each user's normal contacts
- **Real-time detections** for investigation, and alerts in the Defender portal

Plan 1 is included in Microsoft 365 Business Premium; Plan 2 (next lesson) is included in Microsoft 365 E5.

terms.d: Baseline email filtering included with every cloud mailbox.
Detonates attachments in a sandbox before delivery to catch unknown malware.
Time-of-click URL scanning and rewriting in email, Office apps and Teams.
Anti-phishing detection of messages pretending to be specific users or domains.

lessons.trap: Safe Links checks URLs at click time while Safe Attachments sandboxes files; both are Plan 1 features, not Plan 2-only.
lessons.example: An attacker sends a clean link that is switched to a phishing page hours later; Safe Links blocks it when the user clicks.

lessons.title: Defender for Office 365 Plan 2: investigate and respond
lessons.short: Defender for Office 365 Plan 2 includes everything in Plan 1 plus Threat Explorer, Threat Trackers, Campaigns, automated investigation and response (AIR), and Attack simulation training for running realistic phishing simulations.
lessons.deep:
Plan 2 is aimed at security teams that investigate and respond, not only prevent.

- **Threat Explorer** (replaces Real-time detections from Plan 1): search all email, filter by threat type, sender, URL or attachment, and take remediation actions such as soft delete or move to junk.
- **Threat Trackers**: widgets and saved queries that track threats relevant to your organisation.
- **Campaigns**: groups related malicious messages into a coordinated campaign view, showing who was targeted and who clicked.
- **Automated investigation and response (AIR)**: playbooks that investigate an alert (e.g. a user-reported phish), find similar messages and recommend or perform remediation. AIR for compromised users is included.
- **Attack simulation training**: run benign, realistic phishing and other social-engineering simulations, then assign training to users who fell for them.
- **Priority account protection** and advanced hunting over email and Teams data in Defender XDR.

**Licensing**: Plan 2 is included in **Microsoft 365 E5** and Office 365 E5 (and available as add-ons). EOP features such as **ZAP** remain available in every tier.

terms.d: Plan 2 tool to hunt, analyse and remediate email threats.
View grouping related phishing/malware messages into one coordinated attack.
Plan 2 feature that runs simulated phishing attacks and assigns training.

lessons.trap: Plan 1 shows Real-time detections, Plan 2 shows Threat Explorer; attack simulation training and AIR are Plan 2 only.
lessons.example: After a phishing wave, the SOC uses Campaigns to see 400 recipients, removes the messages with Threat Explorer and schedules an attack simulation for the departments that clicked.

lessons.title: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
lessons.short: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint protects devices with attack surface reduction, next-generation protection (Microsoft Defender Antivirus), endpoint detection and response (EDR), automated investigation and remediation, and vulnerability management, across Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS.
lessons.deep:
Defender for Endpoint is an enterprise endpoint security platform. It uses sensors built into Windows (and agents for other platforms) plus Microsoft's cloud analytics.

**Main capabilities**
- **Core Defender Vulnerability Management**: discover devices and software, find vulnerabilities and misconfigurations.
- **Attack surface reduction (ASR)**: shrink the places attackers can get in, e.g. **ASR rules** (block Office apps creating child processes), controlled folder access (ransomware), network protection, exploit protection, device control.
- **Next-generation protection**: **Microsoft Defender Antivirus** with cloud-delivered, behaviour-based protection.
- **Endpoint detection and response (EDR)**: records detailed device behaviour, detects advanced attacks in near real time and lets analysts see process trees and timelines.
- **Automated investigation and remediation**: investigates alerts automatically and fixes issues at scale.
- **Response actions**: **isolate device** (cut it off the network while keeping its connection to the Defender service), run antivirus scan, restrict app execution, collect an investigation package, live response.

**Plans**: **Plan 1** gives prevention (next-gen protection, ASR, device control, manual response). **Plan 2** adds **EDR**, automated investigation and remediation, advanced hunting, core vulnerability management and threat analytics. Microsoft 365 E5 includes Plan 2.

terms.d: Endpoint detection and response: behavioural detection, investigation and response on devices.
Controls and rules that block risky behaviours attackers commonly abuse.
Microsoft Defender Antivirus with cloud and behaviour-based detection.
Response action cutting a device off the network except the Defender service.

lessons.trap: EDR and automated investigation are Plan 2 features; Plan 1 is mainly prevention (antivirus and ASR).
lessons.example: A macro in a Word file tries to launch PowerShell; an ASR rule blocks it, EDR raises an alert, and the analyst isolates the laptop.

lessons.title: Defender for Cloud Apps: CASB and Cloud Discovery
lessons.short: Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps is a cloud access security broker (CASB). It discovers shadow IT with Cloud Discovery, rates apps in its cloud app catalog, and uses app connectors to give visibility and control of sanctioned SaaS apps.
lessons.deep:
A **CASB** sits between users and cloud services to enforce security policy. Microsoft describes the CASB framework as four pillars: **visibility** (find apps and users), **data security** (DLP, sensitivity labels), **threat protection** (detect anomalous behaviour, compromised accounts, malware) and **compliance** (assess apps against regulations).

**Cloud Discovery (shadow IT)**
- Analyses traffic logs from firewalls and proxies (uploaded snapshots or continuous via a log collector), or uses the **Defender for Endpoint integration** to see cloud app use from managed devices, on or off the corporate network.
- Each discovered app is matched against the **cloud app catalog**, which gives a risk score based on many risk factors (security, compliance, legal, general).
- Process: **identify** apps in use, **assess** their risk, **manage** them by tagging **sanctioned** or **unsanctioned** and setting policies. Unsanctioned apps can be blocked on devices onboarded to Defender for Endpoint.

**App connectors** use the SaaS provider's APIs (for example Microsoft 365, Salesforce, Google Workspace, Box) to scan files, activities and configuration in sanctioned apps, with no agent inside the SaaS app.

terms.d: Cloud access security broker: enforces security between users and cloud apps.
Cloud apps used without IT's knowledge or approval.
Defender for Cloud Apps feature that finds cloud apps from traffic/endpoint data.
API integration with a SaaS app for visibility and control.

lessons.trap: Cloud Discovery works from traffic logs or Defender for Endpoint signals; it doesn't need an agent inside each SaaS app.
lessons.example: Cloud Discovery reveals 60 users uploading files to an unapproved file-sharing app with a poor risk score; IT tags it unsanctioned and it is blocked on managed devices.

lessons.title: Defender for Cloud Apps: session control, SSPM and app governance
lessons.short: Conditional Access App Control lets Defender for Cloud Apps monitor and control user sessions in real time, such as blocking downloads on unmanaged devices. SaaS Security Posture Management (SSPM) finds misconfigurations, and app governance protects against risky OAuth apps.
lessons.deep:
**Conditional Access App Control** works with **Microsoft Entra Conditional Access**: Conditional Access routes a user's browser session through Defender for Cloud Apps, which acts as a **reverse proxy**. Then:
- **access policies** allow or block access to the app
- **session policies** monitor activity in real time and can block downloads, protect downloaded files with labels, or block uploads of sensitive content, e.g. only on unmanaged devices

**Other policy types**: activity policies, anomaly detection policies (impossible travel, mass download, ransomware-like activity), file policies (scan files in connected apps for sensitive information) and Cloud Discovery policies.

**SaaS Security Posture Management (SSPM)**: for connected apps, surfaces misconfigurations and recommended settings based on industry standards; these recommendations appear in **Microsoft Secure Score**.

**App governance** (app-to-app protection): many apps use **OAuth** consent to access data on a user's behalf through Microsoft Graph. App governance monitors these apps' permissions, credentials and behaviour, detects overprivileged, unused or anomalous apps, and can disable them.

Defender for Cloud Apps works for Microsoft and non-Microsoft SaaS apps and feeds alerts into Defender XDR incidents.

terms.d: Reverse-proxy session control for cloud apps, driven by Entra Conditional Access.
Real-time monitoring/control of actions (download, upload) inside an app session.
SaaS Security Posture Management: finds misconfigurations in connected SaaS apps.
Monitoring and control of OAuth-enabled apps and their permissions.

lessons.trap: Real-time control of downloads within a session is Conditional Access App Control (session policy), not Cloud Discovery or app connectors.
lessons.example: Contractors on personal laptops can view SharePoint documents in the browser, but a session policy blocks downloading files labelled Confidential.

lessons.title: Microsoft Defender for Identity
lessons.short: Microsoft Defender for Identity uses sensors on domain controllers and identity servers to detect attacks against on-premises Active Directory, such as reconnaissance, compromised credentials, lateral movement and domain dominance, and reports identity security posture.
lessons.deep:
Many attacks end with the attacker controlling Active Directory. **Microsoft Defender for Identity** (formerly Azure Advanced Threat Protection, Azure ATP) watches identity infrastructure to stop that.

**How it works**
- **Sensors** are installed on **domain controllers**, and also on AD FS, AD CS and Microsoft Entra Connect servers. They read network traffic and Windows events locally and send only the needed signals to the cloud service.
- Behavioural analytics learn normal behaviour and flag anomalies. It is managed in the **Microsoft Defender portal**.

**What it detects, by attack stage**
- **Reconnaissance**: user, group, IP and LDAP enumeration
- **Compromised credentials**: brute-force attacks, suspicious authentications
- **Lateral movement**: pass-the-hash, pass-the-ticket
- **Domain dominance**: Golden Ticket, DCSync, DCShadow, malicious replication, remote code execution on domain controllers

**Posture**: **identity security posture assessments** (e.g. unsecure Kerberos delegation, legacy protocols) appear in **Microsoft Secure Score**, and **lateral movement paths** show how an attacker could hop from a normal account to a sensitive one.

Response actions, such as **disabling a user** in AD, can be performed manually or by automatic attack disruption.

terms.d: Defender for Identity component installed on domain controllers and identity servers.
Chain of accounts/devices an attacker could use to reach sensitive accounts.
Forged Kerberos ticket using the KRBTGT key, giving domain-wide access.
Reusing a stolen password hash to authenticate without the password.

lessons.trap: On-premises AD attacks (Golden Ticket, pass-the-hash, LDAP reconnaissance) map to Defender for Identity, not Entra ID Protection, which covers cloud sign-in and user risk.
lessons.example: An attacker on a compromised workstation enumerates Domain Admins via LDAP; Defender for Identity raises a reconnaissance alert linked to the device's EDR alerts.

lessons.title: Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management
lessons.short: Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management continuously discovers devices and software, assesses vulnerabilities and misconfigurations, prioritises them by risk and threat context, and tracks remediation, using the Defender for Endpoint sensor instead of periodic scans.
lessons.deep:
Traditional vulnerability scanning runs on a schedule. **Defender Vulnerability Management** is **continuous** and agent-based: it uses the Defender for Endpoint sensors already on devices.

**Core capabilities** (included in Defender for Endpoint Plan 2 and Defender for Servers)
- **Device discovery and inventory**, **software inventory** and software usage insights
- **Vulnerability assessment** (CVEs) and **security configuration assessment**
- **Risk-based prioritisation**: uses threat intelligence (is it exploited in the wild?), breach likelihood and business value of the device, and exposure score
- **Remediation and tracking**: create **remediation requests**, which can open a ticket in **Microsoft Intune**, or record **exceptions**; track progress

**Premium capabilities** (Defender Vulnerability Management add-on for Plan 2, or the **standalone** offering)
- security baselines assessment
- **block vulnerable applications**
- browser extensions assessment
- digital certificate assessment
- network share analysis
- hardware and firmware assessment

In the Defender portal, vulnerability management sits under **Exposure management**. It supports Windows, macOS, Linux and mobile platforms, and contributes to **Microsoft Secure Score for Devices**.

terms.d: Measure of how exposed your devices are to current threats.
Prioritised remediation action, such as updating a vulnerable app.
Tracked task to fix a weakness; can create an Intune ticket.

lessons.trap: Blocking vulnerable apps and assessing browser extensions/certificates need the premium add-on or standalone, not core Defender for Endpoint Plan 2.
lessons.example: A new Chrome CVE is exploited in the wild; the dashboard ranks it top, shows 300 affected laptops, and the admin raises a remediation request to the Intune team.

lessons.title: Microsoft Threat Intelligence
lessons.short: Microsoft Threat Intelligence turns Microsoft's view of global attacks into context for defenders: threat analytics reports in the Defender portal, threat actor profiles, and indicators of compromise used by Defender XDR and Microsoft Sentinel to detect and enrich threats.
lessons.deep:
Microsoft sees huge volumes of security signals every day across Windows, email, identities and Azure. Its researchers and AI turn that into **threat intelligence (TI)**: knowledge about attackers, their tools and their indicators.

**How you consume it**
- **Threat analytics** in the Microsoft Defender portal: reports written by Microsoft security researchers on active threat actors, campaigns, vulnerabilities and attack techniques. Each report shows an analyst summary, **related incidents**, **impacted assets**, your exposure, and **recommended actions/mitigations**.
- **Threat intelligence in the Defender portal**: Microsoft has consolidated its threat intelligence, including capabilities formerly offered as Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence (MDTI), into a Threat intelligence experience in the Defender portal with an **Overview** page (the threats most relevant to you) and **Intel explorer** (search actors, campaigns, indicators and vulnerabilities), so analysts get TI inside their normal investigations. Entity pages (IPs, domains) show TI context.
- **Microsoft Sentinel**: TI indicators (IPs, domains, URLs, file hashes) can be imported and matched against logs with threat intelligence analytics rules.

**Threat actor naming**: Microsoft uses a weather-themed taxonomy. Families such as **Typhoon** (China), **Blizzard** (Russia), **Sandstorm** (Iran) and **Sleet** (North Korea) identify nation-state actors; **Tempest** marks financially motivated groups; **Storm-** plus a number marks an emerging or developing group.

terms.d: Defender portal reports on active threats with impact and recommended mitigations.
Artifact such as an IP, domain, URL or hash linked to malicious activity.
A person or group conducting attacks, tracked with a Microsoft-assigned name.

lessons.trap: Threat analytics (TI reports) is a different tool from Activity explorer (Purview data activity) and Secure Score (posture).
lessons.example: A threat analytics report on a new ransomware group shows two of your servers are exposed to the exploited CVE and lists the mitigations to apply.

lessons.title: The Microsoft Defender portal
lessons.short: The Microsoft Defender portal (security.microsoft.com) is the single place to manage Defender XDR and Microsoft Sentinel: incidents and alerts, advanced hunting, threat analytics, Microsoft Secure Score, exposure management, the Action center and Security Copilot.
lessons.deep:
The **Microsoft Defender portal** at `https://security.microsoft.com` unifies security operations that used to need many consoles.

**Key areas**
- **Home**: customisable cards showing the security posture and active threats.
- **Incidents & alerts**: one queue of correlated incidents from all Defender services, Entra ID Protection, Purview, Defender for Cloud and Sentinel.
- **Hunting**: **advanced hunting** with KQL, custom detection rules.
- **Actions & submissions**: the **Action center** (pending/completed remediations) and submissions of suspicious email, URLs and files to Microsoft.
- **Threat intelligence**: **threat analytics** and intel profiles.
- **Microsoft Secure Score**: a measurement of security posture with improvement actions for identity, devices, apps and data.
- **Exposure management**: attack surface, critical assets, vulnerability management.
- **Assets, Endpoints, Email & collaboration, Cloud apps, Identities**: product-specific pages and policies.
- **Microsoft Sentinel**: SIEM features (connectors, analytics, workbooks, automation) in the same portal.
- **Microsoft Security Copilot** embedded to summarise incidents, explain scripts and generate KQL.

**Permissions**: Defender XDR **unified role-based access control (RBAC)** lets you manage permissions across workloads in one place, alongside Microsoft Entra roles such as Security Administrator and Security Reader.

Compliance tools (sensitivity labels, eDiscovery) live in the separate **Microsoft Purview portal**.

terms.d: security.microsoft.com, unified console for Defender XDR and Sentinel.
Posture measurement with recommended improvement actions.
Defender XDR permissions model managed centrally across workloads.

lessons.trap: Sensitivity labels and eDiscovery are managed in the Microsoft Purview portal, not the Defender portal.
lessons.example: A SOC analyst starts in the Defender portal incident queue, pivots to advanced hunting, checks a threat analytics report and approves a pending action in the Action center without leaving the portal.

lessons.title: Service Trust Portal offerings
lessons.short: The Service Trust Portal (STP) is Microsoft's library of security, privacy and compliance evidence: independent audit reports (ISO/IEC, SOC, FedRAMP, PCI DSS), whitepapers, pen-test summaries and industry or regional guidance showing how Microsoft cloud services meet standards.
lessons.deep:
When an auditor asks "how do you know Microsoft 365 is secure?", the answer lives in the **Service Trust Portal** (servicetrust.microsoft.com, aka.ms/STP). It proves Microsoft's half of the shared responsibility model.

Main sections:
- **Certifications, Regulations, and Standards**: ISO/IEC, SOC 1/2/3, GDPR, FedRAMP, PCI DSS, CSA STAR and more.
- **Reports, Whitepapers, and Artifacts**: business continuity and DR, **pen test and security assessments**, privacy and data protection, AI resources, FAQs.
- **Industry and Regional Resources**: financial services, healthcare and life sciences, US government, regional material.
- **Resources for your Organization**: documents tied to your tenant's subscription and permissions.
- **My Library**: save documents, subscribe to a series, and set **Notification Settings** to get emails when new versions come out.
- **My Download History**: downloads from the last 18 months.

**Access**: some reports and whitepapers are public. Most need a sign-in with a **Microsoft Entra** work account and acceptance of Microsoft's non-disclosure agreement for compliance materials. **Restricted Documents** need a role such as Compliance Administrator, Security Administrator or Security Reader.

The STP gives you evidence about Microsoft. It doesn't make your tenant compliant; Compliance Manager is where you track your own controls.

terms.d: Microsoft's portal of audit reports, certifications, whitepapers and compliance guides for its cloud services.
Your personal STP page for saved documents, series subscriptions and update email notifications.
STP content available only to users with roles such as Compliance Administrator or Security Reader.

lessons.trap: When a question asks where to get Microsoft's own audit reports, such as SOC 2 or ISO 27001, the answer is the Service Trust Portal, not Compliance Manager or Purview Audit.
lessons.example: A bank's third-party risk team downloads the latest Azure SOC 2 Type 2 report from the STP and saves it to My Library, so they get an email when the next one is published.

lessons.title: Microsoft privacy principles
lessons.short: Microsoft's privacy commitments for its commercial cloud cover four areas: you control your data, you know where it is located, it's secured at rest and in transit, and Microsoft defends it against third-party and government requests.
lessons.deep:
Privacy is about how personal and customer data is collected, used and shared. Microsoft states its commercial cloud commitments as four principles. The Trust Center calls them data control, data location, data security and data defense.

- **You control your data**: your data belongs to you, and you can access, modify or delete it at any time. Microsoft uses it only to provide the services you chose. It doesn't mine customer data for advertising or marketing research. Subprocessors are bound by the same commitments. Microsoft also follows **ISO/IEC 27018**, the code of practice for protecting personal data in the cloud.
- **Know where your data is located**: data residency options in Azure, Microsoft 365 and Dynamics 365 let you choose the geography where data is stored.
- **Your data is secured at rest and in transit**: encryption up to AES-256 at rest, TLS and IPsec in transit, and customer key control with Azure Key Vault.
- **Microsoft defends your data**: government requests should go to you. Microsoft doesn't give any government direct access, and it redirects requests to you and notifies you where the law allows. It challenges requests where it can lawfully do so.

Older study material lists six principles instead: control, transparency, security, strong legal protections, no content-based targeting and benefits to you. The ideas are the same.

terms.d: The geographic location where customer data is stored at rest.
International code of practice for protecting personal data in public clouds.
Microsoft's commitment to redirect and challenge government data requests.

lessons.trap: If a question says Microsoft uses customer content to target ads, it's wrong. Microsoft doesn't use customer data for advertising, and the data stays the customer's.
lessons.example: A police agency asks Microsoft for a company's emails. Microsoft tells the agency to ask the company directly and lets the company know about the request, where the law allows.

lessons.title: Microsoft Purview portal
lessons.short: The Microsoft Purview portal (purview.microsoft.com) is the single place to work with Microsoft Purview data security, data governance, and risk and compliance solutions, with central settings, search, and roles and permissions.
lessons.deep:
**Microsoft Purview** is Microsoft's family of data security, governance and compliance solutions. You manage it in the **Microsoft Purview portal** at https://purview.microsoft.com. This portal replaced the retired **Microsoft Purview compliance portal** (compliance.microsoft.com) and the classic Microsoft Purview governance portal.

What you see:
- **Home page cards**: solution cards, a **Compliance posture status** card fed by Compliance Manager, trials and recommendations, and the **Knowledge Center** with articles, demos and tutorials.
- **Solutions page**: solutions grouped into areas such as Data Security (e.g., Information Protection, Data Loss Prevention, Insider Risk Management), Data Governance (e.g., Unified Catalog, Data Map), and Risk & Compliance (e.g., Compliance Manager, eDiscovery, Audit).
- **Settings**: one central place for portal-wide and solution settings.
- **Roles and permissions**: one place to manage access to Purview.

The portal is permission-aware. Solutions you don't have the role or licence for don't show up as cards. That's why two admins in the same tenant can see different solutions.

terms.d: Unified web portal (purview.microsoft.com) for Purview data security, governance and compliance.
Portal area with Purview articles, demos and tutorials.
Home page card showing progress in Compliance Manager assessments.

lessons.trap: Purview compliance solutions are managed in the Purview portal. The Microsoft Defender portal (security.microsoft.com) and the Microsoft Entra admin center are for security operations and identity.
lessons.example: A compliance admin opens purview.microsoft.com, checks the Compliance posture status card, then goes to Solutions > Data Loss Prevention to review a new policy.

lessons.title: Compliance Manager: controls, assessments, regulations
lessons.short: Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager turns regulations into actionable work. You choose a regulation template, build an assessment of controls, and work through improvement actions. Some controls are Microsoft-managed, some are yours, and some are shared.
lessons.deep:
Compliance Manager is the Purview solution that helps you manage compliance across your multicloud environment, from finding risks to reporting to auditors.

Key elements:
- **Regulations (templates)**: over 360 prebuilt regulatory templates, such as ISO/IEC 27001, NIST CSF and GDPR. You can also build custom ones. Which templates you can use depends on your licensing.
- **Assessments**: a grouping of controls from one regulation, standard or policy, applied to the services in scope. Each assessment has its own score.
- **Controls**: requirements of a regulation. There are three types:
  - **Microsoft-managed**: Microsoft implements them for its cloud services, and you can see implementation details and audit results.
  - **Your controls** (customer-managed): your organization implements them.
  - **Shared controls**: both parties are responsible.
- **Improvement actions**: recommended steps that satisfy controls. You can assign them, test them and attach evidence.

Every tenant starts with the default **Microsoft 365 Data Protection Baseline** assessment. Compliance Manager is the shared responsibility model put into practice.

terms.d: A grouping of controls from one regulation or standard, with its own score.
A requirement of a regulation, standard or policy. It can be Microsoft-managed, yours or shared.
Prebuilt definition of a regulation's controls, used to create an assessment.

lessons.trap: Expect a question on control ownership: Microsoft-managed controls are Microsoft's job and customer-managed controls are yours. Don't mix Compliance Manager assessments up with STP audit reports.
lessons.example: To get ready for ISO/IEC 27001 certification, a team creates an assessment from the ISO 27001 template and assigns its improvement actions to owners.

lessons.title: Improvement actions and automated testing
lessons.short: Improvement actions are the to-do items in Compliance Manager. Each one is technical or nontechnical (documentation or operational), has an implementation status and a test status, stores evidence, and can be tested automatically from Microsoft signals.
lessons.deep:
An **improvement action** tells you exactly what to do to satisfy a control.

**Action types**
- **Technical**: done by changing a configuration in a solution, such as turning on MFA or a DLP policy.
